explanation: Assyria is not an autonomous power, but merely God's disciplinary rod and staff to execute divine judgment upon a hypocritical nation. Isaiah 10:5 (KJV) - "O Assyrian, the rod of mine anger, and the staff in their hand is mine indignation."

question: What proud motivation drives the Assyrian monarch, contradicting God's sovereign purpose in Isaiah 10:7?
opt1: He boasteth that his idols of bronze have delivered the treasures of Damascus into his hand

opt3: He seeketh to establish an eternal kingdom where all peoples shall speak his language
opt4: Howbeit he meaneth not so, neither doth his heart think so; but it is in his heart to destroy and cut off nations not a few
correct: Howbeit he meaneth not so, neither doth his heart think so; but it is in his heart to destroy and cut off nations not a few
explanation: The Assyrian king lacks any conscious desire to serve God's justice; his sole ambition is ruthless conquest, plunder, and the annihilation of nations. Isaiah 10:7 (KJV) - "Howbeit he meaneth not so, neither doth his heart think so; but it is in his heart to destroy and cut off nations not a few."

question: What tool and instrument analogy rebukes the Assyrian king's self-deifying arrogance in Isaiah 10:15?
opt1: Shall the axe boast itself against him that heweth therewith? or shall the saw magnify itself against him that shaketh it?
opt2: Shall the clay say to the potter, What makest thou? or the vessel boast against the furnace?
opt3: Shall the arrow boast against the archer? or the spear claim victory over the warrior?
opt4: Shall the net claim dominion over the fisherman? or the plow over the oxen?

explanation: For an earthly emperor to boast against God is as absurd as an axe boasting over the woodcutter or a saw exalting itself over the carpenter. Isaiah 10:15 (KJV) - "Shall the axe boast itself against him that heweth therewith? or shall the saw magnify itself against him that shaketh it? as if the rod should shake itself against them that lift it up, or as if the staff should lift up itself, as if it were no wood."

question: How will the Light of Israel consume the glory of the Assyrian forest and armed forces in one day in Isaiah 10:17-18?
opt1: A mighty hailstorm shall descend from heaven and break the bronze helmets of his captains
opt2: The light of Israel shall be for a fire, and his Holy One for a flame: and it shall burn and devour his thorns and his briers in one day; and shall consume the glory of his forest, and of his fruitful field, both soul and body
opt3: A great pestilence shall sweep through the camp at midnight and slay all the chariot drivers
opt4: An earthquake shall swallow his baggage train and the waters of the brook shall drown his host
correct: The light of Israel shall be for a fire, and his Holy One for a flame: and it shall burn and devour his thorns and his briers in one day; and shall consume the glory of his forest, and of his fruitful field, both soul and body
explanation: God Himself becomes a consuming flame that completely destroys the Assyrian host, leaving so few survivors that a small child could count them. Isaiah 10:17-19 (KJV) - "And the light of Israel shall be for a fire, and his Holy One for a flame: and it shall burn and devour his thorns and his briers in one day; And shall consume the glory of his forest, and of his fruitful field, both soul and body: and they shall be as when a standardbearer fainteth. And the rest of the trees of his forest shall be few, that a child may write them."

question: Upon whom will the surviving remnant of Israel genuinely lean, abandoning reliance on oppressive foreign powers in Isaiah 10:20?
opt1: They shall trust in the horses of Egypt and the chariots of the Nile

explanation: Having learned the folly of trusting worldly empires that smote them, the remnant will place authentic faith ('stay upon') Yahweh, the Holy One of Israel. Isaiah 10:20 (KJV) - "And it shall come to pass in that day, that the remnant of Israel, and such as are escaped of the house of Jacob, shall no more again stay upon him that smote them; but shall stay upon the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, in truth."

question: Even if the population of Israel be as the sand of the sea, what proportion is divinely ordained to return in Isaiah 10:22?
opt1: All twelve tribes shall inherit the promised land without the loss of a single soul

explanation: Quoted by Paul in Romans 9:27, Isaiah declares that despite vast numerical proliferation, only a faithful remnant will experience salvation amidst overflowing judgment. Isaiah 10:22 (KJV) - "For though thy people Israel be as the sand of the sea, yet a remnant of them shall return: the consumption decreed shall overflow with righteousness."

question: Why will the oppressive Assyrian yoke be broken and removed from the shoulder of God's people in Isaiah 10:27?
opt1: His burden shall be taken away from off thy shoulder, and his yoke from off thy neck, and the yoke shall be destroyed because of the anointing

explanation: The heavy imperial yoke is supernaturally shattered 'because of the anointing' - the Messianic Davidic covenant presence and the Spirit's power. explanation: Isaiah traces Sennacherib's lightning invasion from the north, village by village, culminating at Nob where he insolently shakes his fist at Mount Zion. As yet shall he remain at Nob that day: he shall shake his hand against the mount of the daughter of Zion, the hill of Jerusalem."

question: How does the Lord of hosts halt the mighty Assyrian army just outside the gates of Jerusalem in Isaiah 10:33-34?

opt4: He shall split the earth beneath their siege engines and cast their chariots into the sea

explanation: God acts as the cosmic woodsman, felling the towering Assyrian army like high cedar trees with terrifying suddenness through His angel. correct: There shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots

question: What complete sevenfold endowment of the Holy Spirit rests permanently upon the Messianic Branch in Isaiah 11:2?
opt1: The spirit of prophecy, the spirit of holiness, the spirit of revelation, the spirit of truth, the spirit of grace, the spirit of supplication, and the spirit of glory
opt2: The spirit of kingship, the spirit of victory, the spirit of judgment, the spirit of burning, the spirit of peace, the spirit of liberty, and the spirit of majesty
opt3: The spirit of creation, the spirit of providence, the spirit of faith, the spirit of hope, the spirit of charity, the spirit of endurance, and the spirit of joy
opt4: The spirit of the LORD, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the LORD

explanation: The Messiah possesses the fullness of the Holy Spirit in threefold pairs of divine attributes: wisdom/understanding (intellectual), counsel/might (practical/governing), and knowledge/fear of the LORD (spiritual/relational). Isaiah 11:2 (KJV) - "And the spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the LORD;"

question: How will the Messianic King execute judicial decisions, transcending superficial human perception in Isaiah 11:3-4?
opt1: He shall not judge after the sight of his eyes, neither reprove after the hearing of his ears: but with righteousness shall he judge the poor, and reprove with equity for the meek of the earth: and he shall smite the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips shall he slay the wicked

explanation: Operating with divine discernment, the Messiah champions the defenseless poor and slays the wicked through the sovereign power of His authoritative word. Isaiah 11:3-4 (KJV) - "And shall make him of quick understanding in the fear of the LORD: and he shall not judge after the sight of his eyes, neither reprove after the hearing of his ears: But with righteousness shall he judge the poor, and reprove with equity for the meek of the earth: and he shall smite the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips shall he slay the wicked."

question: What royal garments serve as the waist-girdle of the Messianic King in Isaiah 11:5?
opt1: A belt of beaten gold set with onyx stones and sapphires

opt4: An apron of fine linen adorned with twelve precious gems

explanation: Righteousness and steadfast covenant faithfulness are the foundational virtues girding the Messiah for sovereign, active administration. Isaiah 11:5 (KJV) - "And righteousness shall be the girdle of his loins, and faithfulness the girdle of his reins."

question: What extraordinary zoological reconciliation and cosmic peace will characterize the animal kingdom under Messiah in Isaiah 11:6-8?
opt1: The eagle shall nest with the dove, the falcon shall feed the sparrow, and the hawk shall sing upon the olive tree
opt2: The serpent shall lose its fangs, the dragon shall flee into the abyss, and the leviathan shall praise God in the sea

correct: The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; and the calf and the young lion and the fatling together; and a little child shall lead them; and the sucking child shall play on the hole of the asp
explanation: Predator and prey lose all natural hostility in Edenic harmony: wolves and lambs cohabit, lions eat straw like oxen, and young children safely play near venomous serpents. Isaiah 11:6-8 (KJV) - "The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; and the calf and the young lion and the fatling together; and a little child shall lead them. And the cow and the bear shall feed; their young ones shall lie down together: and the lion shall eat straw like the ox. question: What universal spiritual reality will saturate the earth in the holy mountain of the LORD in Isaiah 11:9?

explanation: Violence and destruction cease completely because experiential, saving knowledge of Yahweh will saturate the globe as completely as waters fill the ocean bed. Isaiah 11:9 (KJV) - "They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain: for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea."

explanation: Quoted in Romans 15:12, this prophecy reveals the root of Jesse elevated as a universal banner, drawing all Gentile nations to find glorious salvation in Him. Isaiah 11:10 (KJV) - "And in that day there shall be a root of Jesse, which shall stand for an ensign of the people; to it shall the Gentiles seek: and his rest shall be glorious."

question: From what vast geographic distribution will the Lord set His hand a second time to recover the remnant of His people in Isaiah 11:11?

explanation: Echoing the first redemption from Egypt (the Exodus), God will perform a second global ingathering of the scattered remnant from across Africa, the Middle East, and Mediterranean coastlands. Isaiah 11:11 (KJV) - "And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Cush, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea."

opt4: The jealousy between the sons of Leah and the sons of Rachel shall be extinguished

explanation: Centuries of bitter regional rivalry and civil warfare between the northern kingdom (Ephraim) and the southern kingdom (Judah) are permanently dissolved in mutual love. Isaiah 11:13 (KJV) - "The envy also of Ephraim shall depart, and the adversaries of Judah shall be cut off: Ephraim shall not envy Judah, and Judah shall not vex Ephraim."

Isaiah 11:15-16 (KJV) - "And the LORD shall utterly destroy the tongue of the Egyptian sea; and with his mighty wind shall he shake his hand over the river, and shall smite it in the seven streams, and make men go over dryshod. And there shall be an highway for the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria; like as it was to Israel in the day that he came up out of the land of Egypt."

question: What personal hymn of reconciled comfort opens the eschatological thanksgiving of Isaiah 12:1?

explanation: Quoting Moses' Song of the Sea (Exodus 15:2), the prophet celebrates that Yahweh Himself is his absolute strength, song, and personal salvation. question: What compound divine name, expressing the eternal self-existent covenant God, appears in Isaiah 12:2?

question: In the liturgical architecture of the Book of Isaiah, what literary role does Chapter 12 fulfill?

question: How are the invading armies summoned by the Lord of hosts described as instruments of divine indignation in Isaiah 13:4-5?

question: What relentless northern nation is specifically stirred up by God to overthrow Babylon, scorning financial bribes in Isaiah 13:17?
opt1: Behold, I will stir up the Medes against them, which shall not regard silver; and as for gold, they shall not delight in it
opt2: Behold, I will summon the Scythians from the steppes, who spare neither young nor old
opt3: Behold, I will bring the Persians from the mountains, who burn palaces with fire
opt4: Behold, I will call the Greeks from across the sea, who shatter bronze armor
correct: Behold, I will stir up the Medes against them, which shall not regard silver; and as for gold, they shall not delight in it
explanation: The Medes (allied with Cyrus the Persian) are unbribable invaders motivated solely by bloodthirsty conquest rather than ransom silver. Isaiah 13:17 (KJV) - "Behold, I will stir up the Medes against them, which shall not regard silver; and as for gold, they shall not delight in it."

question: To what historic catastrophic destruction is the ultimate ruin of Babylon compared in Isaiah 13:19?
opt1: It shall be drowned beneath the sea like the host of Pharaoh at the Red Sea
opt2: And Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, the beauty of the Chaldees' excellency, shall be as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah
opt3: It shall be overthrown like Jericho when the trumpets sounded and the walls fell
opt4: It shall be burned with sulfur like the cities of the plain in the days of Abraham
correct: And Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, the beauty of the Chaldees' excellency, shall be as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah
explanation: The premier imperial metropolis will suffer total, irrecoverable desolation identical to God's historic overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah. Isaiah 13:19 (KJV) - "And Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, the beauty of the Chaldees' excellency, shall be as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah."

question: What absolute, perpetual abandonment will overtake the site of Babylon according to Isaiah 13:20?
opt1: It shall become a quarry of stone for foreign kings, and its bricks shall build palaces in Shushan
opt2: It shall be plowed as a field of barley, and the fishermen of the gulf shall spread nets upon its foundations
opt3: It shall never be inhabited, neither shall it be dwelt in from generation to generation: neither shall the Arabian pitch tent there; neither shall the shepherds make their fold there
opt4: It shall be remembered only in lamentations, and no traveler shall cross its broken canals
correct: It shall never be inhabited, neither shall it be dwelt in from generation to generation: neither shall the Arabian pitch tent there; neither shall the shepherds make their fold there
explanation: The ruins will become so cursed and eerie that even nomadic Bedouins will refuse to pitch tents or fold their flocks there. Isaiah 13:20 (KJV) - "It shall never be inhabited, neither shall it be dwelt in from generation to generation: neither shall the Arabian pitch tent there; neither shall the shepherds make their fold there."

question: What desolate creatures, wild beasts, and demonic dwellers will inhabit Babylon's luxurious palaces in Isaiah 13:21-22?
opt1: Scorpions shall swarm in their bedchambers, vipers shall nest in their throne rooms, and wolves shall howl at midnight
opt2: Ravens shall perch on their broken pillars, jackals shall gnaw their bones, and bats shall fill their ceiling beams
opt3: Locusts shall consume their royal gardens, hyenas shall lair in their gates, and wild boars shall trample their courts
opt4: Wild beasts of the desert shall lie there; and their houses shall be full of doleful creatures; and owls shall dwell there, and satyrs shall dance there; and the wild beasts of the islands shall cry in their desolate houses, and dragons in their pleasant palaces
correct: Wild beasts of the desert shall lie there; and their houses shall be full of doleful creatures; and owls shall dwell there, and satyrs shall dance there; and the wild beasts of the islands shall cry in their desolate houses, and dragons in their pleasant palaces
explanation: Luxury gives way to eerie desolation: owls, ostriches, jackals, wild beasts, and dancing satyrs (desert demons/wild goats) occupy the former royal pavilions. Isaiah 13:21-22 (KJV) - "But wild beasts of the desert shall lie there; and their houses shall be full of doleful creatures; and owls shall dwell there, and satyrs shall dance there. And the wild beasts of the islands shall cry in their desolate houses, and dragons in their pleasant palaces: and her time is near to come, and her days shall not be prolonged."

question: What psychological panic and visceral torment seize the defenders of Babylon when the day of the LORD arrives in Isaiah 13:7-8?
opt1: All hands shall be faint, and every man's heart shall melt: and they shall be afraid: pangs and sorrows shall take hold of them; they shall be in pain as a woman that travaileth: they shall be amazed one at another; their faces shall be as flames
opt2: Their knees shall knock together, their tongues shall cleave to the roof of their mouth, and they shall cast away their weapons
opt3: Their captains shall weep like infants, their mighty men shall stumble in the streets, and their princes shall rend their garments
opt4: A spirit of madness shall drive them into the river, and they shall slay one another in confusion before the gates
correct: All hands shall be faint, and every man's heart shall melt: and they shall be afraid: pangs and sorrows shall take hold of them; they shall be in pain as a woman that travaileth: they shall be amazed one at another; their faces shall be as flames
explanation: Human pride dissolves into paralyzed terror, excruciating labor-like anguish, mutual bewilderment, and flushed faces of despair. Isaiah 13:7-8 (KJV) - "Therefore shall all hands be faint, and every man's heart shall melt: And they shall be afraid: pangs and sorrows shall take hold of them; they shall be in pain as a woman that travaileth: they shall be amazed one at another; their faces shall be as flames."

question: What universal moral arrogance and ruthless tyranny does God vow to permanently terminate in Isaiah 13:11?
opt1: I will break the golden cups of their sorcery and expose their secret abominations
opt2: I will cause the arrogancy of the proud to cease, and will lay low the haughtiness of the terrible
opt3: I will overthrow the astrologers of the Chaldeans and confound their monthly prognosticators
opt4: I will dissolve their trade cartels and sink their merchant ships in the Persian gulf
correct: I will cause the arrogancy of the proud to cease, and will lay low the haughtiness of the terrible
explanation: God targets the core spiritual root of Babylon: imperial hubris, boastful pride, and ruthless oppression of humanity. Isaiah 13:11 (KJV) - "And I will punish the world for their evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; and I will cause the arrogancy of the proud to cease, and will lay low the haughtiness of the terrible."

question: What covenantal restoration and geopolitical reversal awaits Israel following the overthrow of Babylon in Isaiah 14:1-2?
opt1: Israel shall build an empire greater than Solomon's, and all kings shall bring tribute to Jerusalem
opt2: The LORD will have mercy on Jacob, and will yet choose Israel, and set them in their own land: and the strangers shall be joined with them ... and they shall take them captives, whose captives they were; and they shall rule over their oppressors
opt3: The exiles shall return with ten thousand chariots of silver and conquer the coast of the Philistines
opt4: The house of David shall execute vengeance upon all the provinces of the east and burn their temples
correct: The LORD will have mercy on Jacob, and will yet choose Israel, and set them in their own land: and the strangers shall be joined with them ... and they shall take them captives, whose captives they were; and they shall rule over their oppressors
explanation: God re-elects and settles Israel, incorporating gentile converts ('strangers') and turning the tables so former captives rule over their imperial oppressors. Isaiah 14:1-2 (KJV) - "For the LORD will have mercy on Jacob, and will yet choose Israel, and set them in their own land: and the strangers shall be joined with them, and they shall cleave to the house of Jacob ... and they shall take them captives, whose captives they were; and they shall rule over their oppressors."

question: What satirical taunt song (mashal) does Israel take up against the fallen king of Babylon in Isaiah 14:4?
opt1: How art thou broken, O great hammer of the nations!
opt2: Where are thy magicians now, O city of astrologers!
opt3: How hath the oppressor ceased! the golden city ceased!
opt4: Fallen, fallen is the queen of the Euphrates!
correct: How hath the oppressor ceased! the golden city ceased!
explanation: The taunt marvels that the seemingly invincible imperial oppressor and opulent golden city (Babylon) have been brought to an abrupt, absolute end. Isaiah 14:4 (KJV) - "That thou shalt take up this proverb against the king of Babylon, and say, How hath the oppressor ceased! the golden city ceased!"

question: What majestic trees of the forest rejoice at the tyrant's downfall, celebrating their relief from timber-felling in Isaiah 14:8?
opt1: The great oaks of Bashan and the olive trees of Carmel
opt2: The palm trees of Jericho and the willow trees by the watercourses
opt3: The terebinths of Mamre and the sycamores of the lowland plains
opt4: Yea, the fir trees rejoice at thee, and the cedars of Lebanon, saying, Since thou art laid down, no feller is come up against us
correct: Yea, the fir trees rejoice at thee, and the cedars of Lebanon, saying, Since thou art laid down, no feller is come up against us
explanation: Nature personified celebrates: the ancient cedars of Lebanon rejoice because invading Mesopotamian emperors will no longer cut them down for palace timber. Isaiah 14:8 (KJV) - "Yea, the fir trees rejoice at thee, and the cedars of Lebanon, saying, Since thou art laid down, no feller is come up against us."

question: What dramatic underworld reception greets the king of Babylon as he enters Sheol in Isaiah 14:9-10?
opt1: Hell from beneath is moved for thee to meet thee at thy coming: it stirreth up the dead for thee, even all the chief ones of the earth; it hath raised up from their thrones all the kings of the nations. All they shall speak and say unto thee, Art thou also become weak as we? art thou become like unto us?
opt2: The abyss openeth its mouth to consume his chariot, and the kings of the east mock his bronze armor
opt3: The spirits of the giants weep in darkness, and the captains of Assyria bind his soul in iron chains
opt4: The underworld trembleth with thunder, and the shades of Egypt refuse to receive his royal corpse
correct: Hell from beneath is moved for thee to meet thee at thy coming: it stirreth up the dead for thee, even all the chief ones of the earth; it hath raised up from their thrones all the kings of the nations. All they shall speak and say unto thee, Art thou also become weak as we? art thou become like unto us?
explanation: Sheol is personified as a royal hall where deceased monarchs rise from their shadowy thrones to taunt Babylon's emperor on his utter debasement and weakness. Isaiah 14:9-10 (KJV) - "Hell from beneath is moved for thee to meet thee at thy coming: it stirreth up the dead for thee, even all the chief ones of the earth; it hath raised up from their thrones all the kings of the nations. All they shall speak and say unto thee, Art thou also become weak as we? art thou become like unto us?"

question: What famous cosmic lamentation exposes the Luciferian hubris of the king of Babylon in Isaiah 14:12?
opt1: How is the bright star of the dawn plunged into the sea, O prince of the Chaldeans!
opt2: How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning! how art thou cut down to the ground, which didst weaken the nations!
opt3: How hath the mighty angel lost his crown, O ruler of the winged lions!
opt4: How art thou dashed against the rocks of the pit, O sovereign of the northern sky!
correct: How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning! how art thou cut down to the ground, which didst weaken the nations!
explanation: Addressing the Babylonian monarch in terms of the radiant day-star (Helel ben Shachar / Lucifer), the passage details the archetypal pride and fall of Satan behind human tyranny. Isaiah 14:12 (KJV) - "How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning! how art thou cut down to the ground, which didst weaken the nations!"

question: What five audacious 'I will' statements articulate the self-deifying ambition of the fallen monarch in Isaiah 14:13-14?
opt1: I will conquer the kings of the west, I will seize the treasures of Egypt, I will build an eternal city, I will command the angels of heaven, I will reign forever
opt2: I will sit upon the throne of David, I will burn the holy temple, I will drink from golden vessels, I will command the sun to stand still, I will be worshipped by all flesh
opt3: I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God: I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north: I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the most High
opt4: I will bridge the great rivers, I will level the high mountains, I will enslave all nations, I will overthrow the stars, I will declare myself the maker of the world
correct: I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God: I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north: I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the most High
explanation: Five blasphemous declarations reveal absolute pride: ascending heaven, exalting his throne above divine stars, presiding on the divine council mount, ascending the clouds, and equaling the Most High. Isaiah 14:13-14 (KJV) - "For thou hast said in thine heart, I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God: I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north: I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the most High."

question: What shocking contrast exists between the burial of ordinary kings and the desecrated corpse of Babylon's monarch in Isaiah 14:18-19?
opt1: Foreign monarchs are buried in tombs of cut granite, but thy bones shall be dissolved with fire upon the altar of Marduk
opt2: Other kings have royal monuments inscribed with their deeds, but thy memory shall be blotted out under seventy cubits of salt
opt3: The princes of the earth sleep in cedar coffins, but thy flesh shall be cast into the Euphrates to feed the fishes
opt4: All the kings of the nations, even all of them, lie in glory, every one in his own house. But thou art cast out of thy grave like an abominable branch, and as the raiment of those that are slain, thrust through with a sword, that go down to the stones of the pit; as a carcase trodden under feet
correct: All the kings of the nations, even all of them, lie in glory, every one in his own house. But thou art cast out of thy grave like an abominable branch, and as the raiment of those that are slain, thrust through with a sword, that go down to the stones of the pit; as a carcase trodden under feet
explanation: While foreign monarchs receive honorable burial in royal mausoleums, Babylon's king is denied a grave, left rotting on the battlefield like an abominable broken branch. Isaiah 14:18-19 (KJV) - "All the kings of the nations, even all of them, lie in glory, every one in his own house. But thou art cast out of thy grave like an abominable branch, and as the raiment of those that are slain, thrust through with a sword, that go down to the stones of the pit; as a carcase trodden under feet."

question: With what domestic sweeping implement will the Lord of hosts sweep Babylon into eternal desolation in Isaiah 14:23?
opt1: I will sweep it with the besom of destruction, saith the LORD of hosts
opt2: With the fiery shovel of divine fury
opt3: With the heavy iron flail of judgment
opt4: With the great pruning hook of wrath
correct: I will sweep it with the besom of destruction, saith the LORD of hosts
explanation: God dismisses Babylon as mere refuse, sweeping it off the face of the earth with the broom ('besom') of divine destruction. Isaiah 14:23 (KJV) - "I will also make it a possession for the bittern, and pools of water: and I will sweep it with the besom of destruction, saith the LORD of hosts."

question: What sovereign divine oath guarantees that God's eternal purposes can never be disannulled in Isaiah 14:24-27?
opt1: As I live, saith the Lord GOD, I will not relent, neither will I repent, until every word be fulfilled
opt2: The LORD of hosts hath sworn, saying, Surely as I have thought, so shall it come to pass; and as I have purposed, so shall it stand ... For the LORD of hosts hath purposed, and who shall disannul it? and his hand is stretched out, and who shall turn it back?
opt3: Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my covenant with the seed of Abraham shall never fail
opt4: The word that goeth forth out of my mouth shall not return unto me void, but shall prosper
correct: The LORD of hosts hath sworn, saying, Surely as I have thought, so shall it come to pass; and as I have purposed, so shall it stand ... For the LORD of hosts hath purposed, and who shall disannul it? and his hand is stretched out, and who shall turn it back?
explanation: God's sovereign decree is immutable and unstoppable; no human or demonic force can thwart what Yahweh Sabaoth has purposed. Isaiah 14:24, 27 (KJV) - "The LORD of hosts hath sworn, saying, Surely as I have thought, so shall it come to pass; and as I have purposed, so shall it stand ... For the LORD of hosts hath purposed, and who shall disannul it? and his hand is stretched out, and who shall turn it back?"

question: Why is Philistia warned not to rejoice over the death of the Judahite king (or Assyrian smiter) in the year King Ahaz died in Isaiah 14:28-29?
opt1: Because the armies of Egypt shall burn thy five royal cities with brimstone from the sea
opt2: Because the high priest shall blow the silver trumpets and summon the sons of Dan to war
opt3: Rejoice not thou, whole Palestina, because the rod of him that smote thee is broken: for out of the serpent's root shall come forth a cockatrice, and his fruit shall be a fiery flying serpent
opt4: Because the famine shall consume thy olives and a mighty tempest shall sink thy merchant galleys
correct: Rejoice not thou, whole Palestina, because the rod of him that smote thee is broken: for out of the serpent's root shall come forth a cockatrice, and his fruit shall be a fiery flying serpent
explanation: Philistia's celebration over a broken rod is premature: an even more lethal conqueror (Hezekiah or the fierce Assyrian emperors) will arise like a deadly flying serpent to crush them. Isaiah 14:28-29 (KJV) - "In the year that king Ahaz died was this burden. Rejoice not thou, whole Palestina, because the rod of him that smote thee is broken: for out of the serpent's root shall come forth a cockatrice, and his fruit shall be a fiery flying serpent."

question: What twin major fortresses of Moab are laid waste and brought to silence in a single night in Isaiah 15:1?
opt1: Heshbon and Elealeh are destroyed in the night watches
opt2: Dibon and Medeba are consumed with foreign fire
opt3: Ar of Moab is laid waste, and brought to silence; Kir of Moab is laid waste, and brought to silence
opt4: Jahaz and Zoar are overthrown by the eastern whirlwind
correct: Ar of Moab is laid waste, and brought to silence; Kir of Moab is laid waste, and brought to silence
explanation: The sudden nocturnal overthrow of Ar (the ancient capital) and Kir (the premier southern stronghold / Kerak) shatters Moab's defense in a single night. Isaiah 15:1 (KJV) - "The burden of Moab. Because in the night Ar of Moab is laid waste, and brought to silence; because in the night Kir of Moab is laid waste, and brought to silence;"

question: What signs of universal cultural and religious mourning are displayed upon all heads and beards in Moab in Isaiah 15:2?
opt1: On all their heads shall be ashes of the altar, and their beards smeared with dust
opt2: Their foreheads shall be gashed with knives, and their beards plucked out by the roots
opt3: Their hair shall be bound with sackcloth ropes, and their cheeks stained with blood
opt4: On all their heads shall be baldness, and every beard cut off
correct: On all their heads shall be baldness, and every beard cut off
explanation: Shaving the head bald and cutting off the beard were extreme ancient Near Eastern signs of profound national grief, humiliation, and religious despair. Isaiah 15:2 (KJV) - "He is gone up to Bajith, and to Dibon, the high places, to weep: Moab shall howl over Nebo, and over Medeba: on all their heads shall be baldness, and every beard cut off."

question: What public garment of lamentation do the citizens of Moab wear in their streets and upon the flat tops of their houses in Isaiah 15:3?
opt1: In their streets they shall gird themselves with sackcloth: on the tops of their houses, and in their streets, every one shall howl, weeping abundantly
opt2: They shall wear rent garments of purple and cast their jewels into the public cisterns
opt3: They shall clothe themselves in black sheepskins and lie in the ashes of their thresholds
opt4: They shall strip off their embroidered mantles and walk naked through the gates of the city
correct: In their streets they shall gird themselves with sackcloth: on the tops of their houses, and in their streets, every one shall howl, weeping abundantly
explanation: All strata of society don coarse sackcloth, ascending rooftops and gathering in streets to unleash loud wailing. Isaiah 15:3 (KJV) - "In their streets they shall gird themselves with sackcloth: on the tops of their houses, and in their streets, every one shall howl, weeping abundantly."

question: What two northern agricultural cities of Moab cry out so intensely that their grief echoes all the way to Jahaz in Isaiah 15:4?
opt1: Aroer and Kiriathaim shall lift up their voices unto the hills
opt2: Heshbon shall cry, and Elealeh: their voice shall be heard even unto Jahaz
opt3: Beth-gamul and Bozrah shall lament unto the borders of Ammon
opt4: Madmen and Horonaim shall weep even unto the river Arnon
correct: Heshbon shall cry, and Elealeh: their voice shall be heard even unto Jahaz
explanation: The screams of panic from Heshbon and Elealeh carry across the plateau to the military outpost of Jahaz, unnerving even armed warriors. Isaiah 15:4 (KJV) - "And Heshbon shall cry, and Elealeh: their voice shall be heard even unto Jahaz: therefore the armed soldiers of Moab shall cry out; his life shall be grievous unto him."

question: To what animal is the fugitive city or fleeing remnant of Moab compared as refugees escape toward Zoar in Isaiah 15:5?
opt1: A wild ass of the desert
opt2: A hunted roe upon the mountains
opt3: An heifer of three years old
opt4: A wounded lioness in the thicket
correct: An heifer of three years old
explanation: Moab in her prime strength is poignantly pictured as a vigorous young heifer (eglah shelishiyah) now bellowing in terror as she flees southward toward Zoar. Isaiah 15:5 (KJV) - "My heart shall cry out for Moab; his fugitives shall flee unto Zoar, an heifer of three years old: for by the mounting up of Luhith with weeping shall they go it up; for in the way of Horonaim they shall raise up a cry of destruction."

question: What ecological and agrarian catastrophe overtakes the vital springs of Nimrim in Isaiah 15:6?
opt1: The springs of Nimrim are stopped with stones and contaminated with bitter wormwood
opt2: The brooks of Nimrim are dried up by summer drought and trampled by foreign cavalry
opt3: The river of Nimrim is turned to blood and its fish have perished in the reeds
opt4: The waters of Nimrim shall be desolate: for the hay is withered away, the grass faileth, there is no green thing
correct: The waters of Nimrim shall be desolate: for the hay is withered away, the grass faileth, there is no green thing
explanation: The lush oasis waters of Nimrim dry up or are destroyed, causing pasture vegetation, hay, and all green growth to wither into brown dust. Isaiah 15:6 (KJV) - "For the waters of Nimrim shall be desolate: for the hay is withered away, the grass faileth, there is no green thing."

question: Across what southern watercourse do the fleeing refugees carry their remaining rescued wealth and goods in Isaiah 15:7?
opt1: The brook of the willows
opt2: The river Arnon
opt3: The brook Jabbok
opt4: The valley of Zered
correct: The brook of the willows
explanation: Moabite refugees desperately carry their surviving personal treasures across the border stream known as the brook of the willows (Wadi el-Hasa). Isaiah 15:7 (KJV) - "Therefore the abundance they have gotten, and that which they have laid up, shall they carry away to the brook of the willows."

question: What border locations mark the complete perimeter circumference of Moab's echoing wailing in Isaiah 15:8?
opt1: From the mouth of the Arnon even unto the salt sea, and from Zoar unto Mount Nebo
opt2: The cry is gone round about the borders of Moab; the howling thereof unto Eglaim, and the howling thereof unto Beer-elim
opt3: From the gates of Rabbah unto the plains of Moab, and from Aroer unto Kadesh-barnea
opt4: From the high places of Baal-meon unto the rocks of Sela, and from Jahaz to Dibon
correct: The cry is gone round about the borders of Moab; the howling thereof unto Eglaim, and the howling thereof unto Beer-elim
explanation: The cries of agony encompass the entire national frontier, from Eglaim in the south to Beer-elim ('well of the leaders') in the eastern desert. Isaiah 15:8 (KJV) - "For the cry is gone round about the borders of Moab; the howling thereof unto Eglaim, and the howling thereof unto Beer-elim."

question: What horrific contamination fills the waters of Dimon (Dibon), and what predator will hunt down the surviving refugees in Isaiah 15:9?
opt1: The waters of Dimon are turned to gall, and jackals shall feast upon the wounded in the rocks
opt2: The waters of Dimon are dried up, and foreign archers shall pursue the fugitives into Edom
opt3: The waters of Dimon shall be full of blood: for I will bring more upon Dimon, lions upon him that escapeth of Moab, and upon the remnant of the land
opt4: The waters of Dimon are filled with corpses, and vultures shall gather from Mount Seir
correct: The waters of Dimon shall be full of blood: for I will bring more upon Dimon, lions upon him that escapeth of Moab, and upon the remnant of the land
explanation: Massacre turns the stream of Dimon into literal blood, and God brings further judgment: predatory lions (or fierce conquerors) hunting down survivors. Isaiah 15:9 (KJV) - "For the waters of Dimon shall be full of blood: for I will bring more upon Dimon, lions upon him that escapeth of Moab, and upon the remnant of the land."

question: What striking theological feature characterizes Isaiah's posture toward Moab's suffering in Isaiah 15:5?
opt1: The prophet boasts with vindictive triumph over Israel's ancient adversary
opt2: The prophet commands the armies of Judah to plunder the abandoned fields
opt3: The prophet remains indifferent, pronouncing only cold judicial condemnation
opt4: The prophet weeps with profound human empathy and grief ('My heart shall cry out for Moab')
correct: The prophet weeps with profound human empathy and grief ('My heart shall cry out for Moab')
explanation: Unlike pagan oracles of callous celebration, Yahweh's prophet exhibits deep, genuine sorrow over the agony of a neighboring pagan nation. Isaiah 15:5 (KJV) - "My heart shall cry out for Moab; his fugitives shall flee unto Zoar, an heifer of three years old:"

question: What diplomatic tribute is Moab advised to send from the desert fortress of Sela to the Davidic throne in Jerusalem in Isaiah 16:1?
opt1: Send ye talents of refined silver from the mines of Edom to the high priest
opt2: Send ye vessels of bronze and oil of balsam to the palace of the king
opt3: Send ye fine linen and rams of Nebaioth to the temple altar
opt4: Send ye the lamb to the ruler of the land from Sela to the wilderness, unto the mount of the daughter of Zion
correct: Send ye the lamb to the ruler of the land from Sela to the wilderness, unto the mount of the daughter of Zion
explanation: Moab is urged to renew her ancient Davidic vassal tribute (2 Kings 3:4) by sending sheep/lambs from rock-fortress Sela (Petra) to Mount Zion. Isaiah 16:1 (KJV) - "Send ye the lamb to the ruler of the land from Sela to the wilderness, unto the mount of the daughter of Zion."

question: To what helpless creatures are the fleeing daughters of Moab compared at the shallow river crossings in Isaiah 16:2?
opt1: As a wandering bird cast out of the nest, so the daughters of Moab shall be at the fords of Arnon
opt2: As frightened gazelles chased by hunters across the gravel plains
opt3: As sheep scattered on the mountains without a shepherd
opt4: As doves fluttering in the clefts of the cliffs before the eagle
correct: As a wandering bird cast out of the nest, so the daughters of Moab shall be at the fords of Arnon
explanation: Moabite refugee women waiting anxiously at the river Arnon fords resemble terrified fledglings pushed out of their nest into the wilderness. Isaiah 16:2 (KJV) - "For it shall be, that, as a wandering bird cast out of the nest, so the daughters of Moab shall be at the fords of Arnon."

question: What Messianic throne vision in the tabernacle of David is presented as the ultimate refuge of justice and mercy in Isaiah 16:5?
opt1: And upon the high mountain shall the scepter of Judah be lifted up, and all kings shall kiss the son
opt2: And in mercy shall the throne be established: and he shall sit upon it in truth in the tabernacle of David, judging, and seeking judgment, and hasting righteousness
opt3: And the glory of the temple shall be restored with gold, and twelve judges shall sit upon the thrones of Israel
opt4: And the horn of David shall bud in triumph, and the oppressor shall be driven into the outer sea
correct: And in mercy shall the throne be established: and he shall sit upon it in truth in the tabernacle of David, judging, and seeking judgment, and hasting righteousness
explanation: A glorious Messianic promise shines amidst tragedy: a Davidic King whose throne is established on steadfast mercy (chesed), unwavering truth (emet), and prompt justice. Isaiah 16:5 (KJV) - "And in mercy shall the throne be established: and he shall sit upon it in truth in the tabernacle of David, judging, and seeking judgment, and hasting righteousness."

question: What fourfold moral pride of Moab prevented her from finding humble refuge in Judah in Isaiah 16:6?
opt1: His idolatrous worship of Chemosh, his human sacrifices, his treaty with Egypt, and his contempt of the law
opt2: His reliance on high walls, his great wealth of silver, his cavalry of mules, and his boastful scribes
opt3: We have heard of the pride of Moab; he is very proud: even of his haughtiness, and his pride, and his wrath: but his lies shall not be so
opt4: His hatred of Jacob, his mockery of the prophets, his greed for pastures, and his unfaithfulness to treaties

Isaiah 19:5, 7-9 (KJV) - "And the waters shall fail from the sea, and the river shall be wasted and dried up ... The paper reeds by the brooks, by the mouth of the brooks, and every thing sown by the brooks, shall wither, be driven away, and be no more. The fishers also shall mourn ... Moreover they that work in fine flax, and they that weave networks, shall be confounded."

question: What complete intellectual bankruptcy overtakes the famed wise men of Pharaoh in Zoan and Noph in Isaiah 19:11-14?
opt1: The astrologers of Heliopolis have forgotten their charts and cannot interpret the eclipses of the sun
opt2: The scribes have lost their papyrus scrolls and their magicians are struck blind by the angel
opt3: The princes of Zoan are fools, the counsel of the wise counsellors of Pharaoh is become brutish ... the LORD hath mingled a perverse spirit in the midst thereof: and they have caused Egypt to err in every work thereof, as a drunken man staggereth in his vomit
opt4: The physicians cannot heal the plague of boils and their embalmers flee from the royal tombs
correct: The princes of Zoan are fools, the counsel of the wise counsellors of Pharaoh is become brutish ... the LORD hath mingled a perverse spirit in the midst thereof: and they have caused Egypt to err in every work thereof, as a drunken man staggereth in his vomit
explanation: Egypt's renowned royal intelligentsia in Zoan (Tanis) and Noph (Memphis) are reduced to staggering like helpless drunkards due to divinely inflicted confusion. Isaiah 19:11, 14 (KJV) - "Surely the princes of Zoan are fools, the counsel of the wise counsellors of Pharaoh is become brutish ... The LORD hath mingled a perverse spirit in the midst thereof: and they have caused Egypt to err in every work thereof, as a drunken man staggereth in his vomit."

question: How many cities in the land of Egypt will speak the language of Canaan and swear allegiance to Yahweh in Isaiah 19:18?
opt1: Seven cities along the banks of the Nile, and one shall be called the City of Refuge
opt2: Twelve cities in the delta of Egypt, and one shall be called the City of Righteousness
opt3: Ten cities from Alexandria to Thebes, and one shall be called the City of the Sun
opt4: Five cities in the land of Egypt speak the language of Canaan, and swear to the LORD of hosts; one shall be called, The city of destruction
correct: Five cities in the land of Egypt speak the language of Canaan, and swear to the LORD of hosts; one shall be called, The city of destruction
explanation: Five Egyptian urban centers will embrace the Hebrew language of covenant worship and pledge loyalty to Yahweh Sabaoth (one known as the City of the Sun / City of Destruction / Ir ha-Heres). Isaiah 19:18 (KJV) - "In that day shall five cities in the land of Egypt speak the language of Canaan, and swear to the LORD of hosts; one shall be called, The city of destruction."

question: What physical monuments of covenantal worship and divine witness will be erected in Egypt in Isaiah 19:19-20?
opt1: An altar to the LORD in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar at the border thereof to the LORD. And it shall be for a sign and for a witness unto the LORD of hosts in the land of Egypt
opt2: A holy temple of cut cedar on the island of Elephantine and twelve bronze lamps in Memphis
opt3: A golden mercy seat in the palace of Pharaoh and a tabernacle in the wilderness of Shur
opt4: A memorial stone engraved with the Ten Commandments upon the highest pyramid of Giza
correct: An altar to the LORD in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar at the border thereof to the LORD. And it shall be for a sign and for a witness unto the LORD of hosts in the land of Egypt
explanation: An authentic sacrificial altar in the heart of Egypt and a commemorative pillar at its frontier testify to Egypt's full covenantal conversion to Yahweh. Isaiah 19:19-20 (KJV) - "In that day shall there be an altar to the LORD in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar at the border thereof to the LORD. And it shall be for a sign and for a witness unto the LORD of hosts in the land of Egypt: for they shall cry unto the LORD because of the oppressors, and he shall send them a saviour, and a great one, and he shall deliver them."

question: How does the LORD respond when converted Egyptians cry out under oppression in Isaiah 19:20-22?
opt1: He shall send the twelve tribes of Israel to drive their enemies into the Red Sea
opt2: He shall send them a saviour, and a great one, and he shall deliver them ... the LORD shall smite Egypt: he shall smite and heal it: and they shall return even to the LORD, and he shall be intreated of them, and shall heal them
opt3: He shall raise up an anointed Pharaoh from the lineage of Joseph to rule them in peace
opt4: He shall cause the waters of the Nile to turn into sweet milk to nourish their households
correct: He shall send them a saviour, and a great one, and he shall deliver them ... the LORD shall smite Egypt: he shall smite and heal it: and they shall return even to the LORD, and he shall be intreated of them, and shall heal them
explanation: Egypt experiences the same redemptive pattern as Israel: crying out under oppression, receiving a divine Saviour/Deliverer, and being smitten only to be healed upon repentance. Isaiah 19:20, 22 (KJV) - "And he shall send them a saviour, and a great one, and he shall deliver them ... And the LORD shall smite Egypt: he shall smite and heal it: and they shall return even to the LORD, and he shall be intreated of them, and shall heal them."

question: What international reconciliation highway unites ancient imperial arch-enemies in shared worship in Isaiah 19:23?
opt1: A military canal linking the Mediterranean with the Red Sea to trade silver with Tarshish
opt2: A royal road guarded by the cavalry of Judah from Damascus unto the river of Babylon
opt3: There shall be a highway out of Egypt to Assyria, and the Assyrian shall come into Egypt, and the Egyptian into Assyria, and the Egyptians shall serve with the Assyrians
opt4: A caravan route through the wilderness of Sinai where all kings shall pay tribute
correct: There shall be a highway out of Egypt to Assyria, and the Assyrian shall come into Egypt, and the Egyptian into Assyria, and the Egyptians shall serve with the Assyrians
explanation: The ultimate geopolitical miracle of the gospel: traditional mortal enemies Egypt and Assyria are united via a holy highway, traveling freely and worshiping Yahweh together. Isaiah 19:23 (KJV) - "In that day shall there be a highway out of Egypt to Assyria, and the Assyrian shall come into Egypt, and the Egyptian into Assyria, and the Egyptians shall serve with the Assyrians."

question: What revolutionary threefold benediction incorporates Gentile superpowers into the covenant family of God in Isaiah 19:24-25?
opt1: Blessed be Zion the city of peace, and Babylon the footstool of my feet, and Jacob my servant
opt2: Blessed be Judah my lawgiver, and Edom my washpot, and Philistia my conquered land
opt3: Blessed be the seed of Abraham, and the islands of the Gentiles, and the holy temple forever
opt4: Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel mine inheritance
correct: Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel mine inheritance
explanation: In an astonishing expansion of covenant blessing, God confers Israel's exclusive titles upon her former oppressors: Egypt is called 'my people,' Assyria 'the work of my hands,' and Israel 'mine inheritance.' Isaiah 19:24-25 (KJV) - "In that day shall Israel be the third with Egypt and with Assyria, even a blessing in the midst of the land: Whom the LORD of hosts shall bless, saying, Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel mine inheritance."

question: What military campaign under Sargon king of Assyria provides the precise historical setting for the prophetic action in Isaiah 20:1?
opt1: In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah when Sennacherib laid siege to Lachish
opt2: In the year that Shalmaneser besieged Samaria and carried the ten tribes into exile
opt3: In the year that Tiglath-pileser invaded Galilee and captured the cities of Naphtali
opt4: In the year that Tartan came unto Ashdod, (when Sargon the king of Assyria sent him,) and fought against Ashdod, and took it
correct: In the year that Tartan came unto Ashdod, (when Sargon the king of Assyria sent him,) and fought against Ashdod, and took it
explanation: In 711 BC, Sargon II sent his commander-in-chief (the Tartan) to capture the rebellious Philistine fortress city of Ashdod. Isaiah 20:1 (KJV) - "In the year that Tartan came unto Ashdod, (when Sargon the king of Assyria sent him,) and fought against Ashdod, and took it;"

question: What shocking prophetic sign-act was Isaiah commanded to perform as a living sermon in Isaiah 20:2?
opt1: Go and loose the sackcloth from off thy loins, and put off thy shoe from thy foot. And he did so, walking naked and barefoot
opt2: Take an iron pan and set it for an iron wall between thee and the city of Jerusalem
opt3: Lie upon thy left side three hundred and ninety days, bearing the iniquity of the house of Israel
opt4: Shave thy head and beard with a barber's razor and weigh the hair in the balances
correct: Go and loose the sackcloth from off thy loins, and put off thy shoe from thy foot. And he did so, walking naked and barefoot
explanation: Isaiah discarded his customary prophet's mantle of sackcloth and sandals, dressing only in a captive's loincloth ('naked and barefoot') as a visual prophecy. Isaiah 20:2 (KJV) - "At the same time spake the LORD by Isaiah the son of Amoz, saying, Go and loose the sackcloth from off thy loins, and put off thy shoe from thy foot. And he did so, walking naked and barefoot."

question: For how long did Isaiah walk naked and barefoot as a sign and wonder upon Egypt and Ethiopia in Isaiah 20:3?
opt1: Forty days
opt2: Three years
opt3: Seventy days
opt4: Seven years
correct: Three years
explanation: For three full years (714-711 BC), Isaiah walked stripped and barefoot as a dramatic visual warning against relying on Egypt and Ethiopia. Isaiah 20:3 (KJV) - "And the LORD said, Like as my servant Isaiah hath walked naked and barefoot three years for a sign and wonder upon Egypt and upon Ethiopia;"

question: What humiliating captivity of Egypt and Ethiopia by the king of Assyria was symbolized by Isaiah's attire in Isaiah 20:4?
opt1: The princes of Egypt shall be bound in bronze chains and forced to dig the canals of Nineveh
opt2: The warriors of Ethiopia shall be blinded with hot irons and sold as slaves in the market of Calah
opt3: The king of Assyria shall lead away the Egyptians prisoners, and the Ethiopians captives, young and old, naked and barefoot, even with their buttocks uncovered, to the shame of Egypt
opt4: The daughters of Pharaoh shall be made handmaids to the queens of Assyria in foreign palaces
correct: The king of Assyria shall lead away the Egyptians prisoners, and the Ethiopians captives, young and old, naked and barefoot, even with their buttocks uncovered, to the shame of Egypt
explanation: Assyrian conquerors marched deportees naked and barefoot, exposing their buttocks to inflict total psychological humiliation upon proud African empires. Isaiah 20:4 (KJV) - "So shall the king of Assyria lead away the Egyptians prisoners, and the Ethiopians captives, young and old, naked and barefoot, even with their buttocks uncovered, to the shame of Egypt."

question: How will the pro-Egyptian political faction in Judah react when their expected ally collapses in Isaiah 20:5?
opt1: They shall rend their clothes and offer fifty talents of silver to the king of Babylon
opt2: They shall flee into the caves of the rocks and make covenant with the Philistines
opt3: They shall accuse the prophet of treason and cast him into the dungeon of Malchiah
opt4: And they shall be afraid and ashamed of Ethiopia their expectation, and of Egypt their glory
correct: And they shall be afraid and ashamed of Ethiopia their expectation, and of Egypt their glory
explanation: Judahite politicians who foolishly boasted in Egyptian military might will be filled with acute shame and panic at its total failure. Isaiah 20:5 (KJV) - "And they shall be afraid and ashamed of Ethiopia their expectation, and of Egypt their glory."

question: What despairing question will the inhabitants of the Philistine/Levantine coastland ('this isle') utter in Isaiah 20:6?
opt1: Behold, such is our expectation, whither we flee for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria: and how shall we escape?
opt2: Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? and have they delivered Samaria out of his hand?
opt3: Can a man hide himself in secret places that the king of Assyria shall not find him?
opt4: Why did we not pay tribute of gold to the emperor before our towers were broken down?
correct: Behold, such is our expectation, whither we flee for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria: and how shall we escape?
explanation: Small coastal states realize the impossibility of escaping Assyrian conquest after witnessing the total collapse of their superpower protector, Egypt. Isaiah 20:6 (KJV) - "And the inhabitant of this isle shall say in that day, Behold, such is our expectation, whither we flee for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria: and how shall we escape?"

question: What military office did the 'Tartan' hold in the imperial hierarchy of Assyria mentioned in Isaiah 20:1?
opt1: The chief royal astrologer and reader of liver omens
opt2: The supreme commander-in-chief or field marshal of the royal Assyrian armed forces
opt3: The governor of the western provinces across the Euphrates
opt4: The royal cupbearer and private treasurer of the emperor
correct: The supreme commander-in-chief or field marshal of the royal Assyrian armed forces
explanation: Tartan (Turtanu) is the official Akkadian title for the supreme commander of the Assyrian army, second only to the king. Isaiah 20:1 (KJV) - "In the year that Tartan came unto Ashdod, (when Sargon the king of Assyria sent him,) and fought against Ashdod, and took it;"

question: Why did King Hezekiah contemplate joining the rebellion of Ashdod against Sargon II?
opt1: To capture the maritime port of Ashdod and expand Judah's commercial trade to Tarshish
opt2: To avenge the death of his father King Ahaz at the hands of the Philistine lords
opt3: To exploit Egyptian promises of military intervention and free Judah from paying annual Assyrian tribute
opt4: To install a Davidic prince upon the throne of the five cities of the Philistines
correct: To exploit Egyptian promises of military intervention and free Judah from paying annual Assyrian tribute
explanation: Ashdod rebelled against Assyria in 711 BC with Egyptian backing, tempting Judah to join; Isaiah's dramatic three-year sign dissuaded Hezekiah from joining this suicidal alliance. Isaiah 20:1-6 (KJV) - "At the same time spake the LORD by Isaiah the son of Amoz ... walking naked and barefoot three years for a sign and wonder upon Egypt and upon Ethiopia;"

question: What theological lesson does Isaiah 20 teach regarding human political and military alliances?
opt1: Prophets should not interfere in the foreign policy decisions of the royal cabinet
opt2: Small nations must always submit to larger pagan empires without seeking freedom
opt3: Military treaties with African nations are inherently forbidden under Levitical law
opt4: Putting trust in worldly superpowers rather than in the living God leads to catastrophic shame, disappointment, and enslavement
correct: Putting trust in worldly superpowers rather than in the living God leads to catastrophic shame, disappointment, and enslavement
explanation: The sign-act demonstrates the futility of human alliances: relying on fleshly glory ('Egypt their glory') ends in naked shame, while trusting Yahweh secures true protection. Isaiah 20:5 (KJV) - "And they shall be afraid and ashamed of Ethiopia their expectation, and of Egypt their glory."

question: What does the phrase 'walking naked and barefoot' specifically signify regarding Isaiah's physical condition?
opt1: Wearing only an inner loincloth or undergarment, stripped of his outer prophetic mantle of haircloth/sackcloth like a captive slave
opt2: Completely devoid of all clothing in public scandal before the elders
opt3: Clothed in transparent linen imported from the merchants of Alexandria
opt4: Wearing ceremonial sackcloth painted white to resemble the skin of a leper
correct: Wearing only an inner loincloth or undergarment, stripped of his outer prophetic mantle of haircloth/sackcloth like a captive slave
explanation: In biblical idiom, 'naked' (arom) often denotes being stripped down to a minimal undergarment/tunic, dressed like an impoverished slave or war captive. Isaiah 20:2 (KJV) - "And he did so, walking naked and barefoot."

question: What cryptic geographical title introduces the second oracle concerning the fall of Babylon in Isaiah 21:1?
opt1: The burden of the desert of the sea
opt2: The burden of the valley of vision
opt3: The burden of the wilderness of Kedar
opt4: The burden of the waters of Dimon
correct: The burden of the desert of the sea
explanation: Babylon's marshy, flat southern alluvial plain bordering the Persian Gulf is poetically designated 'the desert of the sea.' Isaiah 21:1 (KJV) - "The burden of the desert of the sea. As whirlwinds in the south pass through; so it cometh from the desert, from a terrible land."

question: What two allied eastern nations are summoned to march against Babylon in the vision of Isaiah 21:2?
opt1: Go up, O Assyria: besiege, O Syria
opt2: Go up, O Elam: besiege, O Media; all the sighing thereof have I made to cease
opt3: Go up, O Parthia: besiege, O Armenia
opt4: Go up, O Egypt: besiege, O Ethiopia
correct: Go up, O Elam: besiege, O Media; all the sighing thereof have I made to cease
explanation: Elam (Persia) and Media are commanded to execute divine judgment, ending the grief and sighing caused by Babylonian tyranny. Isaiah 21:2 (KJV) - "A grievous vision is declared unto me; the treacherous dealer dealeth treacherously, and the spoiler spoileth. Go up, O Elam: besiege, O Media; all the sighing thereof have I made to cease."

question: What festive night of royal revelry was suddenly turned into nightmare and terror in Isaiah 21:4-5?
opt1: The night of the new moon feast was turned into darkness, and the wine cups were spilled
opt2: The banquet of the princes was interrupted by lightning, and the golden throne was split
opt3: The night of my pleasure hath he turned into fear unto me. Prepare the table, watch in the watchtower, eat, drink: arise, ye princes, and anoint the shield
opt4: The wedding of the king's daughter was silenced by mourning, and the music ceased
correct: The night of my pleasure hath he turned into fear unto me. Prepare the table, watch in the watchtower, eat, drink: arise, ye princes, and anoint the shield
explanation: Foreshadowing Belshazzar's fateful banquet (Daniel 5), decadent partygoers feast and drink until sudden alarm commands them to oil leather shields for battle. Isaiah 21:4-5 (KJV) - "My heart panted, fearfulness affrighted me: the night of my pleasure hath he turned into fear unto me. Prepare the table, watch in the watchtower, eat, drink: arise, ye princes, and anoint the shield."

question: What animal caravan riders did the vigilant watchman observe approaching from the desert in Isaiah 21:7?
opt1: A troop of mules bearing archers, and fifty war elephants from the east
opt2: A fleet of swift horses from Egypt, and chariots of iron from Damascus
opt3: A company of desert riders upon dromedaries, bearing spears of bronze
opt4: A chariot with a couple of horsemen, a chariot of asses, and a chariot of camels; and he hearkened diligently with much heed
correct: A chariot with a couple of horsemen, a chariot of asses, and a chariot of camels; and he hearkened diligently with much heed
explanation: The watchman spots military messengers mounted in pairs on horses, donkeys, and camels, riding hard with news from the eastern front. Isaiah 21:7 (KJV) - "And he saw a chariot with a couple of horsemen, a chariot of asses, and a chariot of camels; and he hearkened diligently with much heed:"

question: What famous historic announcement of imperial downfall is proclaimed by the approaching watchman in Isaiah 21:9?
opt1: Babylon is fallen, is fallen; and all the graven images of her gods he hath broken unto the ground
opt2: Nineveh is laid waste, who will bemoan her? her gates are burned with fire
opt3: Tyre is sunk into the heart of the seas, and her merchants lament upon the shore
opt4: Egypt is broken like a bruised reed, and Pharaoh's crown is cast into the dust
correct: Babylon is fallen, is fallen; and all the graven images of her gods he hath broken unto the ground
explanation: Echoed in Revelation 14:8 and 18:2, the watchman proclaims the catastrophic, double downfall of Babylon and the smashing of all her manufactured deities. Isaiah 21:9 (KJV) - "And, behold, here cometh a chariot of men, with a couple of horsemen. And he answered and said, Babylon is fallen, is fallen; and all the graven images of her gods he hath broken unto the ground."

question: What tender agricultural title does Isaiah address to his battered, suffering people in exile in Isaiah 21:10?
opt1: O my vineyard planted on the fruitful hill, whose branches have been trampled
opt2: O my threshing, and the corn of my floor: that which I have heard of the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, have I declared unto you
opt3: O my flock scattered upon the mountains, whose shepherd was smitten
opt4: O my olive tree shaken in the storm, whose fruit was gleaned by strangers
correct: O my threshing, and the corn of my floor: that which I have heard of the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, have I declared unto you
explanation: Isaiah addresses Israel as God's threshed grain - crushed and pounded by imperial oppression, yet refined as precious wheat for the divine granary. Isaiah 21:10 (KJV) - "O my threshing, and the corn of my floor: that which I have heard of the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, have I declared unto you."

question: What urgent nocturnal query is called out of Seir (Edom) to the sentinel in the burden of Dumah in Isaiah 21:11?
opt1: Watchman, is the enemy at the gate? Watchman, when will the trumpet sound?
opt2: Watchman, how far is the morning? Watchman, will the storm pass away?
opt3: Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?
opt4: Watchman, where is the star of dawn? Watchman, what seest thou in the desert?
correct: Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?
explanation: A terrified voice from Mount Seir repeatedly calls to the prophet across the dark night of historical calamity: 'Watchman, what of the night?' Isaiah 21:11 (KJV) - "The burden of Dumah. He calleth to me out of Seir, Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?"

question: What enigmatic, double-edged answer does the watchman return to Edom in Isaiah 21:12?
opt1: The dawn shall bring no light, but a deeper darkness shall swallow thy high rocks
opt2: The day of vengeance is at hand, and no man shall escape the sword of the Medes
opt3: The night is far spent, and the sun of righteousness shall arise with healing
opt4: The morning cometh, and also the night: if ye will enquire, enquire ye: return, come
correct: The morning cometh, and also the night: if ye will enquire, enquire ye: return, come
explanation: The sentinel answers cryptically: relief (morning) is followed immediately by renewed tribulation (night); genuine repentance ('return, come') is the only recourse. Isaiah 21:12 (KJV) - "The watchman said, The morning cometh, and also the night: if ye will enquire, enquire ye: return, come."

question: What nomadic oasis inhabitants are commanded to bring bread and water to desperate refugees fleeing the sword in Isaiah 21:14?
opt1: The inhabitants of the land of Tema brought water to him that was thirsty, they prevented with their bread him that fled
opt2: The merchants of Sheba brought gold and spices to the fugitives of the desert
opt3: The sons of Ishmael opened their tents and shared dates from their palm groves
opt4: The shepherds of Midian slaughtered lambs for the fleeing archers of Kedar
correct: The inhabitants of the land of Tema brought water to him that was thirsty, they prevented with their bread him that fled
explanation: The oasis dwellers of Tema in northern Arabia are urged to offer hospitality (bread and water) to merchant caravans (Dedanites) fleeing the ravages of war. Isaiah 21:14 (KJV) - "The inhabitants of the land of Tema brought water to him that was thirsty, they prevented with their bread him that fled."

question: Within what exact duration will all the martial glory and famous archers of Kedar be decimated in Isaiah 21:16-17?
opt1: Within three years, according to the days of a contract labourer
opt2: Within a year, according to the years of an hireling, and all the glory of Kedar shall fail: and the residue of the number of archers, the mighty men of the children of Kedar, shall be diminished
opt3: Within seven months, before the winter rains replenish the dry cisterns
opt4: Within forty days, when the Assyrian cavalry shall surround their oases
correct: Within a year, according to the years of an hireling, and all the glory of Kedar shall fail: and the residue of the number of archers, the mighty men of the children of Kedar, shall be diminished
explanation: Like a hired laborer counting down his exact 365-day contract, the formidable nomadic archers of Kedar will face military decimation within a single year. Isaiah 21:16-17 (KJV) - "For thus hath the Lord said unto me, Within a year, according to the years of an hireling, and all the glory of Kedar shall fail: And the residue of the number of archers, the mighty men of the children of Kedar, shall be diminished: for the LORD God of Israel hath spoken it."

question: What paradoxical title introduces the oracle of judgment against frivolous, unrepentant Jerusalem in Isaiah 22:1?
opt1: The burden of the mountain of the temple
opt2: The burden of the valley of vision
opt3: The burden of the city of David
opt4: The burden of the holy sanctuary
correct: The burden of the valley of vision
explanation: Jerusalem, surrounded by valleys and blessed with prophetic revelation ('vision'), is ironically titled 'the valley of vision' because of spiritual blindness. Isaiah 22:1 (KJV) - "The burden of the valley of vision. What aileth thee now, that thou art wholly gone up to the housetops?"

question: What shocking, cowardly casualty status characterizes Jerusalem's slain men in Isaiah 22:2-3?
opt1: Thy valiant soldiers fell defending the gates, and thy captains were pierced with bronze spears
opt2: Thy youth were consumed by pestilence, and thy elders starved upon the ramparts
opt3: Thy slain men are not slain with the sword, nor dead in battle. All thy rulers are fled together, they are bound by the archers: all that are found in thee are bound together, which have fled from far
opt4: Thy princes were betrayed by foreign mercenaries, and thy archers cast away their bows
correct: Thy slain men are not slain with the sword, nor dead in battle. All thy rulers are fled together, they are bound by the archers: all that are found in thee are bound together, which have fled from far
explanation: The leaders and warriors did not die heroically in combat; they fled in panic and were ignominiously captured and bound without firing a shot. Isaiah 22:2-3 (KJV) - "Thy slain men are not slain with the sword, nor dead in battle. All thy rulers are fled together, they are bound by the archers: all that are found in thee are bound together, which have fled from far."

question: How does Isaiah react to the frivolous, celebrating citizens, refusing their superficial consolations in Isaiah 22:4?
opt1: Rejoice with me, O daughters of Zion, for the siege hath been lifted by the north wind
opt2: Blow the trumpet in the gates and proclaim a fast of forty days before the altar
opt3: Gird on your swords, ye princes of Judah, and charge into the camp of the uncircumcised
opt4: Look away from me; I will weep bitterly, labour not to comfort me, because of the spoiling of the daughter of my people
correct: Look away from me; I will weep bitterly, labour not to comfort me, because of the spoiling of the daughter of my people
explanation: Isaiah refuses to join the premature municipal celebrations, demanding to be left alone to weep bitter tears over the ultimate destruction of his people. Isaiah 22:4 (KJV) - "Therefore said I, Look away from me; I will weep bitterly, labour not to comfort me, because of the spoiling of the daughter of my people."

question: What foreign mercenary archers and cavalrymen filled the pleasant valleys around Jerusalem in Isaiah 22:6-7?
opt1: And Elam bare the quiver with chariots of men and horsemen, and Kir uncovered the shield. And it shall come to pass, that thy choicest valleys shall be full of chariots
opt2: The chariots of Egypt encamped at the pool of Siloam, and the slingers of Ammon at the gate
opt3: The cavalry of Babylon occupied the mount of Olives, and the archers of Syria besieged Zion
opt4: The spearmen of Edom fortified the hill of Gareb, and the horsemen of Tyre secured the pass
correct: And Elam bare the quiver with chariots of men and horsemen, and Kir uncovered the shield. And it shall come to pass, that thy choicest valleys shall be full of chariots
explanation: Auxiliary units serving in the Assyrian army - Elamite archers with quivers and troops from Kir unmasking bronze shields - choke Jerusalem's perimeter valleys. Isaiah 22:6-7 (KJV) - "And Elam bare the quiver with chariots of men and horsemen, and Kir uncovered the shield. And it shall come to pass, that thy choicest valleys shall be full of chariots, and the horsemen shall set themselves in array at the gate."

question: What practical military preparations did Jerusalem frantically undertake during the siege while completely ignoring God in Isaiah 22:8-11?
opt1: Ye hired Egyptian mercenaries with silver from the temple, forged ten thousand bronze swords, and burned the suburbs
opt2: Ye looked to the armour of the house of the forest, gathered the waters of the lower pool, numbered the houses of Jerusalem to break down houses to fortify the wall, and made a ditch between the two walls for the water of the old pool: but ye have not looked unto the maker thereof
opt3: Ye built a second wall of cut stone, filled the royal storehouses with grain from Egypt, and fasted in sackcloth
opt4: Ye closed the iron gates of the citadel, sent ambassadors to Babylon, and cast lots for the captains of the host
correct: Ye looked to the armour of the house of the forest, gathered the waters of the lower pool, numbered the houses of Jerusalem to break down houses to fortify the wall, and made a ditch between the two walls for the water of the old pool: but ye have not looked unto the maker thereof
explanation: The citizens engaged in frantic secular engineering (securing weapons, channeling water, demolishing houses to repair walls) without ever seeking Yahweh, the sovereign Architect of history. Isaiah 22:8-11 (KJV) - "Thou didst look in that day to the armour of the house of the forest. Ye have seen also the breaches of the city of David, that they were many: and ye gathered together the waters of the lower pool. And ye have numbered the houses of Jerusalem, and the houses have ye broken down to fortify the wall. Ye made also a ditch between the two walls for the water of the old pool: but ye have not looked unto the maker thereof, neither had respect unto him that fashioned it long ago."

question: What nihilistic, hedonistic slogan did the ungodly populace chant when God called them to repentance and mourning in Isaiah 22:12-13?
opt1: Great is the temple of the Lord, we shall never be moved
opt2: Let the king save us, for in his horses is our deliverance
opt3: Let us eat and drink; for to morrow we shall die
opt4: Peace, peace, when there is no peace in the gates
correct: Let us eat and drink; for to morrow we shall die
explanation: When God summoned the nation to brokenness and sackcloth, they indulged in fatalistic hedonism, slaughtering cattle and drinking wine with the cynical cry: 'Let us eat and drink; for to morrow we shall die.' Isaiah 22:12-13 (KJV) - "And in that day did the Lord GOD of hosts call to weeping, and to mourning, and to baldness, and to girding with sackcloth: And behold joy and gladness, slaying oxen, and killing sheep, eating flesh, and drinking wine: let us eat and drink; for to morrow we shall die."

question: What terrifying divine sentence of unpardonable iniquity was revealed in Isaiah's ears concerning this reckless rebellion in Isaiah 22:14?
opt1: Thou shalt be carried away captive into Babylon for seventy years of sorrow
opt2: The sword of the king of Assyria shall not depart from thy house forever
opt3: Thy children shall beg for water in the streets and none shall pity them
opt4: Surely this iniquity shall not be purged from you till ye die, saith the Lord GOD of hosts
correct: Surely this iniquity shall not be purged from you till ye die, saith the Lord GOD of hosts
explanation: Hardened, willful cynicism amidst imminent divine judgment crosses a fatal spiritual boundary, remaining unatoned until physical death. Isaiah 22:14 (KJV) - "And it was revealed in mine ears by the LORD of hosts, Surely this iniquity shall not be purged from you till ye die, saith the Lord GOD of hosts."

question: What arrogant self-aggrandizing monument was Shebna the royal steward carving for himself on high in Isaiah 22:15-16?
opt1: What hast thou here? and whom hast thou here, that thou hast hewed thee out a sepulchre here, as he that heweth him out a sepulchre on high, and that graveth an habitation for himself in a rock?
opt2: A golden statue of himself set up in the court of the palace
opt3: An ivory throne inlaid with sapphires from the mountains of Ophir
opt4: A high tower of granite overlooking the king's private gardens
correct: What hast thou here? and whom hast thou here, that thou hast hewed thee out a sepulchre here, as he that heweth him out a sepulchre on high, and that graveth an habitation for himself in a rock?
explanation: Shebna, a self-important palace administrator, ostentatiously carved an aristocratic rock-hewn tomb for himself on the sacred heights of Jerusalem. Isaiah 22:15-16 (KJV) - "Go, get thee unto this treasurer, even unto Shebna, which is over the house, and say, What hast thou here? and whom hast thou here, that thou hast hewed thee out a sepulchre here, as he that heweth him out a sepulchre on high, and that graveth an habitation for himself in a rock?"

question: To what playful athletic object does God compare the disgraced Shebna being hurled violently into exile in Isaiah 22:18?
opt1: He shall cast thee down like a broken potsherd into the valley of Hinnom
opt2: He will surely violently turn and toss thee like a ball into a large country: there shalt thou die
opt3: He shall sweep thee away like a stone cast from a sling into the great deep
opt4: He shall scatter thy bones like dry leaves driven by the autumn wind
correct: He will surely violently turn and toss thee like a ball into a large country: there shalt thou die
