Behold, I will send a blast upon him, and he shall hear a rumour, and return to his own land; and I will cause him to fall by the sword in his own land."

question: What did King Hezekiah do with the blasphemous, threatening letter from Sennacherib in Isaiah 37:14?
opt1: Hezekiah read it before the seventy elders of the gate and commanded an immediate fast
opt2: Hezekiah tore the letter into pieces and cast the fragments into the valley of Hinnom
opt3: Hezekiah went up unto the house of the LORD, and spread it before the LORD
opt4: Hezekiah sent the letter by swift messengers to the pharaoh of Egypt for counsel
correct: Hezekiah went up unto the house of the LORD, and spread it before the LORD
explanation: In supreme faith and vulnerability, Hezekiah carried the threatening parchment into the temple, spreading it out before the ark of the covenant in prayer. Isaiah 37:14 (KJV) - "And Hezekiah received the letter from the hand of the messengers, and read it: and Hezekiah went up unto the house of the LORD, and spread it before the LORD."

question: How did Hezekiah open his prayer, confessing Yahweh's absolute and exclusive sovereignty over all creation in Isaiah 37:16?
opt1: Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised in the city of David, in the mountain of his holiness
opt2: O God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, look down from thy holy habitation and deliver thy heritage
opt3: Lord God Almighty, who didst divide the Red Sea before our fathers, hear the cry of thy servants
opt4: O LORD of hosts, God of Israel, that dwellest between the cherubims, thou art the God, even thou alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth: thou hast made heaven and earth
correct: O LORD of hosts, God of Israel, that dwellest between the cherubims, thou art the God, even thou alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth: thou hast made heaven and earth
explanation: Hezekiah addresses Yahweh Sabaoth enthroned between the cherubim, affirming strict monotheism: He alone is God over all kingdoms because He created heaven and earth. Isaiah 37:16 (KJV) - "O LORD of hosts, God of Israel, that dwellest between the cherubims, thou art the God, even thou alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth: thou hast made heaven and earth."

question: How did the virgin daughter of Zion personified respond to Sennacherib's proud invasion in Isaiah 37:22?
opt1: The virgin, the daughter of Zion, hath despised thee, and laughed thee to scorn; the daughter of Jerusalem hath shaken her head at thee
opt2: The daughter of Zion hath trembled before thy cavalry, and hath fled into the mountain caves
opt3: The daughter of Jerusalem hath wept at the gate, and cast ashes upon her golden hair
opt4: The virgin of Zion hath called upon the angels of heaven to break the bronze chariots of Assyria
correct: The virgin, the daughter of Zion, hath despised thee, and laughed thee to scorn; the daughter of Jerusalem hath shaken her head at thee
explanation: Zion, guarded by her divine King, mocks the invading emperor with defiant laughter and shaking of her head at his futile threats. Isaiah 37:22 (KJV) - "This is the word which the LORD hath spoken concerning him; The virgin, the daughter of Zion, hath despised thee, and laughed thee to scorn; the daughter of Jerusalem hath shaken her head at thee."

question: What animal subjugation metaphor does God use to describe how He will turn Sennacherib back to Nineveh in Isaiah 37:29?
opt1: I will put an iron yoke upon thy neck, and lead thee like a captive ox to the slaughter
opt2: I will put my hook in thy nose, and my bridle in thy lips, and I will turn thee back by the way by which thou camest
opt3: I will bind thy feet with bronze fetters, and drag thee behind the chariots of the host
opt4: I will clip thy wings like an eagle, and cast thee into the deep pit of the desert
correct: I will put my hook in thy nose, and my bridle in thy lips, and I will turn thee back by the way by which thou camest
explanation: Using the very torture Assyrian kings inflicted on captives, God treats Sennacherib like a wild, subdued beast, putting a hook in his nose and a bit in his mouth to drag him home. Isaiah 37:29 (KJV) - "Because thy rage against me, and thy tumult, is come up into mine ears, therefore will I put my hook in thy nose, and my bridle in thy lips, and I will turn thee back by the way by which thou camest."

question: What agricultural sign of remnant restoration was given to Hezekiah covering three consecutive years in Isaiah 37:30-31?
opt1: For three years the clouds shall rain manna, and in the fourth year the olive harvest shall be doubled in the land
opt2: This year the vineyards of Sibmah shall revive, next year the barley of Rephaim shall yield tenfold, and the third year peace shall reign
opt3: Ye shall eat this year such as groweth of itself; and the second year that which springeth of the same: and in the third year sow ye, and reap, and plant vineyards, and eat the fruit thereof. And the remnant that is escaped of the house of Judah shall again take root downward, and bear fruit upward
opt4: For three years the storehouses of Egypt shall provide wheat, and in the third year the exiles shall return with gold
correct: Ye shall eat this year such as groweth of itself; and the second year that which springeth of the same: and in the third year sow ye, and reap, and plant vineyards, and eat the fruit thereof. And the remnant that is escaped of the house of Judah shall again take root downward, and bear fruit upward
explanation: Judah survives on wild growth during war's disruption, resumes normal agrarian cultivation in the third year, and the remnant takes deep spiritual root and bears abundant fruit. Isaiah 37:30-31 (KJV) - "And this shall be a sign unto thee, Ye shall eat this year such as groweth of itself; and the second year that which springeth of the same: and in the third year sow ye, and reap, and plant vineyards, and eat the fruit thereof. And the remnant that is escaped of the house of Judah shall again take root downward, and bear fruit upward:"

question: What absolute military protection does God decree concerning Jerusalem during Sennacherib's siege in Isaiah 37:33-35?
opt1: His battering rams shall not breach the wall, though his archers slay a thousand men upon the ramparts
opt2: He shall encamp for forty days, but his soldiers shall be unable to drink the water of the pool
opt3: He shall burn the outer gates with fire, but the holy sanctuary shall remain untouched by the sword
opt4: He shall not come into this city, nor shoot an arrow there, nor come before it with shields, nor cast a bank against it ... for I will defend this city to save it for mine own sake, and for my servant David's sake
correct: He shall not come into this city, nor shoot an arrow there, nor come before it with shields, nor cast a bank against it ... for I will defend this city to save it for mine own sake, and for my servant David's sake
explanation: Sennacherib was barred from firing a single arrow, advancing with shields, or building a siege ramp against Jerusalem; God defended it for His own glory and David's covenant. Isaiah 37:33, 35 (KJV) - "Therefore thus saith the LORD concerning the king of Assyria, He shall not come into this city, nor shoot an arrow there, nor come before it with shields, nor cast a bank against it ... For I will defend this city to save it for mine own sake, and for my servant David's sake."

question: How many Assyrian soldiers did the angel of the LORD slay in a single night outside Jerusalem in Isaiah 37:36?
opt1: A hundred and fourscore and five thousand (185,000)
opt2: Fifty thousand
opt3: One hundred and twenty thousand
opt4: Two hundred and fifty thousand
correct: A hundred and fourscore and five thousand (185,000)
explanation: The angel of the LORD executed catastrophic overnight destruction, slaughtering 185,000 elite Assyrian troops and leaving their camp filled with dead corpses by morning. Isaiah 37:36 (KJV) - "Then the angel of the LORD went forth, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians a hundred and fourscore and five thousand: and when they arose early in the morning, behold, they were all dead corpses."

question: How was Sennacherib assassinated upon returning to Nineveh in Isaiah 37:37-38?
opt1: While banqueting with his princes, his cupbearer poisoned his wine, and his brother seized the crown
opt2: As he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god, Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword; and they escaped into the land of Armenia: and Esarhaddon his son reigned in his stead
opt3: While reviewing his chariot legions, an arrow shot at a venture pierced his breastplate
opt4: During an earthquake in Nineveh, the stone ceiling of his palace collapsed upon his bed
correct: As he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god, Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword; and they escaped into the land of Armenia: and Esarhaddon his son reigned in his stead
explanation: Sennacherib was murdered by his own patricidal sons (Adrammelech and Sharezer) inside the temple of his god Nisroch, proving the total impotence of his idol. Isaiah 37:38 (KJV) - "And it came to pass, as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god, that Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword; and they escaped into the land of Armenia: and Esarhaddon his son reigned in his stead."

question: What terminal prophetic prognosis did Isaiah deliver to King Hezekiah when he was mortally sick in Isaiah 38:1?
opt1: Prepare a sepulchre in the garden of Uzza: for thy breath faileth before the evening
opt2: Set thine house in order: for thou shalt die, and not live
opt3: Anoint thy son Manasseh king upon thy throne: for the days of thy pilgrimage are ended
opt4: Call the elders of the priests to offer a sin offering: for thy sickness is unto death
correct: Set thine house in order: for thou shalt die, and not live
explanation: Isaiah delivered the blunt divine message: Hezekiah was commanded to settle his royal affairs because his illness was terminal. Isaiah 38:1 (KJV) - "In those days was Hezekiah sick unto death. And Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz came unto him, and said unto him, Thus saith the LORD, Set thine house in order: for thou shalt die, and not live."

question: How did Hezekiah immediately respond to the death sentence, pleading his covenant integrity in Isaiah 38:2-3?
opt1: Hezekiah rent his clothes, cast ashes upon his head, and summoned the seventy elders to intercede
opt2: Hezekiah commanded the priests to sacrifice fifty rams at the bronze altar and wept before the veil
opt3: Then Hezekiah turned his face toward the wall, and prayed unto the LORD, and said, Remember now, O LORD, I beseech thee, how I have walked before thee in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done that which is good in thy sight. And Hezekiah wept sore
opt4: Hezekiah dispatched swift messengers to bring the holy anointing oil from the sanctuary of Shiloh
correct: Then Hezekiah turned his face toward the wall, and prayed unto the LORD, and said, Remember now, O LORD, I beseech thee, how I have walked before thee in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done that which is good in thy sight. And Hezekiah wept sore
explanation: Hezekiah turned his face to the wall in private, passionate agony, weeping bitterly and appealing to his sincere, wholehearted covenant loyalty. Isaiah 38:2-3 (KJV) - "Then Hezekiah turned his face toward the wall, and prayed unto the LORD, And said, Remember now, O LORD, I beseech thee, how I have walked before thee in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done that which is good in thy sight. And Hezekiah wept sore."

question: How many years did God graciously add to Hezekiah's life in response to his prayer and tears in Isaiah 38:5?
opt1: Seven years
opt2: Ten years
opt3: Twenty years
opt4: Fifteen years
correct: Fifteen years
explanation: Moved by Hezekiah's tears, God extended the king's life by an additional 15 years and promised deliverance from Assyria. Isaiah 38:5 (KJV) - "Go, and say to Hezekiah, Thus saith the LORD, the God of David thy father, I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears: behold, I will add unto thy days fifteen years."

question: What miraculous astronomical sign confirmed God's promise to heal Hezekiah in Isaiah 38:7-8?
opt1: Behold, I will bring again the shadow of the degrees, which is gone down in the sun dial of Ahaz, ten degrees backward. So the sun returned ten degrees, by which degrees it was gone down
opt2: The sun stood still in the midst of heaven for a whole day as in the valley of Ajalon
opt3: A rainbow of seven colors appeared over the temple for three days and three nights
opt4: The morning star shone seven times brighter than the sun at noonday
correct: Behold, I will bring again the shadow of the degrees, which is gone down in the sun dial of Ahaz, ten degrees backward. So the sun returned ten degrees, by which degrees it was gone down
explanation: God performed a supernatural cosmic miracle: the shadow on the sundial (steps) of Ahaz reversed ten intervals backward. Isaiah 38:8 (KJV) - "Behold, I will bring again the shadow of the degrees, which is gone down in the sun dial of Ahaz, ten degrees backward. So the sun returned ten degrees, by which degrees it was gone down."

question: To what transient nomadic dwelling does Hezekiah compare his departing lifespan in his poetic writing in Isaiah 38:12?
opt1: As a shadow that declineth upon the wall, and as a vapor that vanisheth before the sun
opt2: Mine age is departed, and is removed from me as a shepherd's tent: I have cut off like a weaver my life: he will cut me off with pining sickness
opt3: As a leaf that falleth from the sycamore, and as a broken reed swept away by the river
opt4: As a garment eaten by moths, and as an earthen vessel shattered upon the stones
correct: Mine age is departed, and is removed from me as a shepherd's tent: I have cut off like a weaver my life: he will cut me off with pining sickness
explanation: Hezekiah likens life's fragility to a nomad's temporary tent struck and moved in an instant, or a finished cloth suddenly severed from the loom. Isaiah 38:12 (KJV) - "Mine age is departed, and is removed from me as a shepherd's tent: I have cut off like a weaver my life: he will cut me off with pining sickness: from day even to night wilt thou make an end of me."

question: What bird vocalizations characterize Hezekiah's mournful prayer in his mortal affliction in Isaiah 38:14?
opt1: Like an owl in the desert did I cry, and like a pelican in the wilderness did I groan
opt2: Like an eagle wounded on the crags did I scream, and like a sparrow on the housetop was I desolate
opt3: Like a crane or a swallow, so did I chatter: I did mourn as a dove: mine eyes fail with looking upward: O LORD, I am oppressed; undertake for me
opt4: Like a raven did I wander in the darkness, and like a turtledove did I weep for my mate
correct: Like a crane or a swallow, so did I chatter: I did mourn as a dove: mine eyes fail with looking upward: O LORD, I am oppressed; undertake for me
explanation: Hezekiah compares his weak, dying gasps to the twittering of cranes and swallows, and his deep sorrow to the cooing mourning of a dove. Isaiah 38:14 (KJV) - "Like a crane or a swallow, so did I chatter: I did mourn as a dove: mine eyes fail with looking upward: O LORD, I am oppressed; undertake for me."

question: What marvelous theological metaphor expresses God's total, unconditional pardon of Hezekiah's sins in Isaiah 38:17?
opt1: Thou hast washed away my guilt in the river of life, and my stains are whiter than snow
opt2: Thou hast blotted out my transgressions from the book of remembrance with the blood of the altar
opt3: Thou hast buried mine iniquities in the deepest abyss of the sea, never to be found
opt4: Thou hast in love to my soul delivered it from the pit of corruption: for thou hast cast all my sins behind thy back
correct: Thou hast in love to my soul delivered it from the pit of corruption: for thou hast cast all my sins behind thy back
explanation: God's love rescues the soul from decay and dismisses sin entirely: casting all human transgressions 'behind His back' where they are forgotten. Isaiah 38:17 (KJV) - "Behold, for peace I had great bitterness: but thou hast in love to my soul delivered it from the pit of corruption: for thou hast cast all my sins behind thy back."

question: Why does Hezekiah celebrate physical survival over the silence of the grave in Isaiah 38:18-19?
opt1: For the grave cannot praise thee, death can not celebrate thee: they that go down into the pit cannot hope for thy truth. The living, the living, he shall praise thee, as I do this day: the father to the children shall make known thy truth
opt2: For in Sheol there is no memory of gold, and the dead cannot divide the inheritance of the land
opt3: For foreign kings cannot worship in the pit, and the princes of the earth lie down in silence
opt4: For the dust cannot build the temple of the Lord, nor can the shadow offer morning sacrifices
correct: For the grave cannot praise thee, death can not celebrate thee: they that go down into the pit cannot hope for thy truth. The living, the living, he shall praise thee, as I do this day: the father to the children shall make known thy truth
explanation: In Old Testament perspective, earthly life provides the vital arena for public, generational praise of Yahweh: the living celebrate God's faithfulness and transmit truth to children. Isaiah 38:18-19 (KJV) - "For the grave cannot praise thee, death can not celebrate thee: they that go down into the pit cannot hope for thy truth. The living, the living, he shall praise thee, as I do this day: the father to the children shall make known thy truth."

question: What physical medicinal poultice did Isaiah prescribe to draw out the infection of Hezekiah's fatal boil in Isaiah 38:21?
opt1: Let them apply oil of myrrh and balsam from Gilead upon the wound
opt2: Let them take a lump of figs, and lay it for a plaister upon the boil, and he shall recover
opt3: Let them wash the flesh seven times in the pool of Siloam with hyssop
opt4: Let them sprinkle salt and frankincense from the altar upon his skin
correct: Let them take a lump of figs, and lay it for a plaister upon the boil, and he shall recover
explanation: Isaiah combined supernatural divine healing with practical ancient medicine: a compress/poultice of compressed dried figs laid upon the inflamed ulcer. Isaiah 38:21 (KJV) - "For Isaiah had said, Let them take a lump of figs, and lay it for a plaister upon the boil, and he shall recover."

question: What was Hezekiah's primary yearning and query regarding his recovery in Isaiah 38:22?
opt1: What is the sign that the king of Assyria shall not return to destroy Jerusalem?
opt2: When shall I sit again upon the throne of David to judge the people?
opt3: What is the sign that I shall go up to the house of the LORD?
opt4: How long shall peace and prosperity endure within my palaces?
correct: What is the sign that I shall go up to the house of the LORD?
explanation: Hezekiah's supreme priority was not mere physical survival or political power, but returning to the house of the LORD to offer public worship. Isaiah 38:22 (KJV) - "Hezekiah also had said, What is the sign that I shall go up to the house of the LORD?"

question: What Babylonian monarch sent ambassadors, letters, and gifts to Hezekiah following his miraculous recovery in Isaiah 39:1?
opt1: Nebuchadnezzar, the son of Nabopolassar, king of Babylon
opt2: Evil-merodach, the prince of the Chaldeans
opt3: Merodach-baladan, the son of Baladan, king of Babylon
opt4: Belshazzar, the co-regent of Babylon
correct: Merodach-baladan, the son of Baladan, king of Babylon
explanation: Merodach-baladan II (Marduk-apla-iddina), the rebel Chaldean ruler seeking anti-Assyrian allies, sent envoys to Hezekiah under the guise of congratulating him on his recovery. Isaiah 39:1 (KJV) - "At that time Merodach-baladan, the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a present to Hezekiah: for he had heard that he had been sick, and was recovered."

question: What comprehensive inventory of royal treasures did Hezekiah ostentatiously display to the Babylonian envoys in Isaiah 39:2?
opt1: The ark of the covenant, the golden menorah, the table of shewbread, and the breastplate of Urim
opt2: The stables of five thousand horses, the chariots of bronze, and the armory of King David
opt3: The royal records of the temple, the books of the law, and the golden scepter of Solomon
opt4: The house of his precious things, the silver, and the gold, and the spices, and the precious ointment, and all the house of his armour, and all that was found in his treasures: there was nothing in his house, nor in all his dominion, that Hezekiah shewed them not
correct: The house of his precious things, the silver, and the gold, and the spices, and the precious ointment, and all the house of his armour, and all that was found in his treasures: there was nothing in his house, nor in all his dominion, that Hezekiah shewed them not
explanation: Flattered by the embassy, Hezekiah succumbed to foolish vanity, displaying every palace treasure: silver, gold, spices, fine oils, military armory, and national wealth. Isaiah 39:2 (KJV) - "And Hezekiah was glad of them, and shewed them the house of his precious things, the silver, and the gold, and the spices, and the precious ointment, and all the house of his armour, and all that was found in his treasures: there was nothing in his house, nor in all his dominion, that Hezekiah shewed them not."

question: How did Hezekiah answer Isaiah's probing question regarding the origin of the foreign visitors in Isaiah 39:3?
opt1: They are come from a far country unto me, even from Babylon
opt2: They came from the islands of Chittim to buy olive oil and wine
opt3: They are ambassadors from Egypt seeking a covenant against Assyria
opt4: They came from the mountains of Media bearing gifts for the temple
correct: They are come from a far country unto me, even from Babylon
explanation: Hezekiah boasted in the prestige of receiving an embassy from a distant, exotic superpower: 'They are come from a far country unto me, even from Babylon.' Isaiah 39:3 (KJV) - "Then came Isaiah the prophet unto king Hezekiah, and said unto him, What said these men? and from whence came they unto thee? And Hezekiah said, They are come from a far country unto me, even from Babylon."

question: What chilling prophecy of Babylonian plunder and exile did Isaiah announce to Hezekiah in Isaiah 39:5-6?
opt1: The king of Assyria shall return with two hundred thousand men and burn Jerusalem with fire
opt2: Behold, the days come, that all that is in thine house, and that which thy fathers have laid up in store until this day, shall be carried to Babylon: nothing shall be left, saith the LORD
opt3: Thy silver shall be cast into the Euphrates and thy palaces leveled by the Medes
opt4: The pharaoh of Egypt shall seize thy daughters and confiscate the treasures of David
correct: Behold, the days come, that all that is in thine house, and that which thy fathers have laid up in store until this day, shall be carried to Babylon: nothing shall be left, saith the LORD
explanation: Isaiah delivers a monumental prophecy over a century in advance: everything Hezekiah proudly displayed will be looted and deported to Babylon. Isaiah 39:5-6 (KJV) - "Then said Isaiah to Hezekiah, Hear the word of the LORD of hosts: Behold, the days come, that all that is in thine house, and that which thy fathers have laid up in store until this day, shall be carried to Babylon: nothing shall be left, saith the LORD."

question: What personal, humiliating fate was prophesied regarding Hezekiah's own royal descendants in Isaiah 39:7?
opt1: They shall be slain with the sword before the eyes of the king of Assyria
opt2: They shall be blinded with hot irons and imprisoned in the fortress of Carchemish
opt3: And of thy sons that shall issue from thee, which thou shalt beget, shall they take away; and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon
opt4: They shall be sold as bondmen to till the fields of the Chaldeans in Shinar
correct: And of thy sons that shall issue from thee, which thou shalt beget, shall they take away; and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon
explanation: Hezekiah's royal offspring (fulfilled in Daniel and his companions, Daniel 1:3-7) will be castrated and made court eunuchs in Babylon's imperial palace. Isaiah 39:7 (KJV) - "And of thy sons that shall issue from thee, which thou shalt beget, shall they take away; and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon."

question: What shortsighted, self-relieved reaction did King Hezekiah express in response to Isaiah's judgment oracle in Isaiah 39:8?
opt1: Alas, my lord! let this evil fall upon me, and spare the children of my house
opt2: The Lord is righteous, but my soul is grieved for the generations to come
opt3: I will repent in sackcloth, if peradventure the Lord will turn away his fierce wrath
opt4: Good is the word of the LORD which thou hast spoken. He said moreover, For there shall be peace and truth in my days
correct: Good is the word of the LORD which thou hast spoken. He said moreover, For there shall be peace and truth in my days
explanation: Hezekiah submitted to God's word, yet exhibited narrow relief that the catastrophe would not occur during his own lifetime: 'there shall be peace and truth in my days.' Isaiah 39:8 (KJV) - "Then said Hezekiah to Isaiah, Good is the word of the LORD which thou hast spoken. He said moreover, For there shall be peace and truth in my days."

question: In the literary and historical architecture of the Book of Isaiah, what critical watershed role does Chapter 39 fulfill?
opt1: It marks the grand transition from the Assyrian crisis (Chapters 1-39) to the Babylonian exile and glorious restoration (Chapters 40-66)
opt2: It concludes the biographical memoirs of the prophet Isaiah before his martyrdom under Manasseh
opt3: It provides the historical treaty documentation between the united monarchy and the Chaldean empire
opt4: It introduces the legal codes for reforming the Levitical priesthood in post-exilic Jerusalem
correct: It marks the grand transition from the Assyrian crisis (Chapters 1-39) to the Babylonian exile and glorious restoration (Chapters 40-66)
explanation: Isaiah 39 forms the structural hinge of the entire book: naming Babylon as the future instrument of exile, paving the way for Chapter 40's opening message of comfort. Isaiah 39:6-7 (KJV) - "Behold, the days come, that all that is in thine house ... shall be carried to Babylon: nothing shall be left, saith the LORD."

question: What spiritual failure lay at the root of Hezekiah's excessive hospitality toward the Babylonian envoys according to 2 Chronicles 32:31?
opt1: He was deceived by foreign sorcery and drank wine laced with Egyptian herbs
opt2: God left him, to try him, that he might know all that was in his heart, exposing pride in his worldly wealth rather than boasting in Yahweh
opt3: He sought to purchase Babylonian cavalry to invade the northern territory of Ephraim
opt4: He desired to arrange a royal marriage between his daughter and the prince of Babylon
correct: God left him, to try him, that he might know all that was in his heart, exposing pride in his worldly wealth rather than boasting in Yahweh
explanation: Hezekiah failed a crucial test of character: instead of bearing witness to Yahweh who miraculously healed him and destroyed Sennacherib, he boasted in material treasures. Isaiah 39:2 (KJV) - "And Hezekiah was glad of them, and shewed them the house of his precious things ... there was nothing in his house, nor in all his dominion, that Hezekiah shewed them not."

question: What contrast exists between Hezekiah's response to Sennacherib's threat (Chapter 37) and his response to Babylon's flattery (Chapter 39)?
opt1: He trusted God against Assyria, but allied with Babylon through animal sacrifices
opt2: He wept sore before Sennacherib, but laughed with scorn before Merodach-baladan
opt3: He resisted military intimidation through humble prayer in the temple, but collapsed before diplomatic flattery and vanity in his palace
opt4: He consulted Isaiah against Assyria, but banished the prophet when Babylon arrived
correct: He resisted military intimidation through humble prayer in the temple, but collapsed before diplomatic flattery and vanity in his palace
explanation: Hezekiah demonstrated spiritual greatness when facing mortal danger and military terror, but was seduced by royal flattery, luxury, and pride of possession. Isaiah 39:2, 8 (KJV) - "And Hezekiah was glad of them, and shewed them the house of his precious things ... Good is the word of the LORD which thou hast spoken."

question: What was the ultimate historical fulfillment of Isaiah's prophecy concerning the treasures and royalty of Judah being carried to Babylon?
opt1: The capture of Jerusalem by Tiglath-pileser III during the Syro-Ephraimite war
opt2: The raid of Shishak king of Egypt who plundered the golden shields of Solomon
opt3: The destruction of the second temple by the Roman legions under Titus in 70 AD
opt4: The Babylonian sieges and final conquest of Jerusalem under Nebuchadnezzar in 586 BC, carrying away temple treasures and Davidic princes
correct: The Babylonian sieges and final conquest of Jerusalem under Nebuchadnezzar in 586 BC, carrying away temple treasures and Davidic princes
explanation: Over a century later (586 BC), Nebuchadnezzar fulfilled this prophecy verbatim, looting all palace/temple wealth and deporting the royal seed to Babylon. Isaiah 39:6-7 (KJV) - "Behold, the days come, that all that is in thine house ... shall be carried to Babylon: nothing shall be left, saith the LORD."

question: What tender, double divine imperative of comfort opens the second major division of the Book of Isaiah in Isaiah 40:1-2?
opt1: Awake, awake; put on thy strength, O Zion; put on thy beautiful garments, O Jerusalem, the holy city
opt2: Arise, shine; for thy light is come, and the glory of the LORD is risen upon thee in the wilderness
opt3: Sing, O barren, thou that didst not bear; break forth into singing, and cry aloud, thou that didst not travail
opt4: Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God. Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem, and cry unto her, that her warfare is accomplished, that her iniquity is pardoned: for she hath received of the LORD's hand double for all her sins
correct: Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God. Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem, and cry unto her, that her warfare is accomplished, that her iniquity is pardoned: for she hath received of the LORD's hand double for all her sins
explanation: Isaiah 40 opens with God's gracious commission (Nachamu, nachamu ami) proclaiming that Jerusalem's hard servitude is completed and her sin fully expiated. Isaiah 40:1-2 (KJV) - "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God. Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem, and cry unto her, that her warfare is accomplished, that her iniquity is pardoned: for she hath received of the LORD's hand double for all her sins."

question: What heraldic wilderness commission prepares the royal causeway for the manifestation of Yahweh's glory in Isaiah 40:3-5?
opt1: The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the LORD, make straight in the desert a highway for our God. Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low: and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places plain: And the glory of the LORD shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together
opt2: Blow ye the trumpet in Zion, and sound an alarm in my holy mountain: let all the inhabitants of the land tremble
opt3: Cast up, cast up the highway; gather out the stones; lift up a standard for the people from the ends of the earth
opt4: Behold, I send my messenger before thy face, which shall prepare thy way before thee: the Lord whom ye seek shall suddenly come
correct: The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the LORD, make straight in the desert a highway for our God. Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low: and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places plain: And the glory of the LORD shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together
explanation: Fulfilled by John the Baptist (Matthew 3:3), this herald calls for spiritual highway construction (leveling mountains of pride, raising valleys of despair) for the arrival of divine glory. Isaiah 40:3-5 (KJV) - "The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the LORD, make straight in the desert a highway for our God. Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low: and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places plain: And the glory of the LORD shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together: for the mouth of the LORD hath spoken it."

question: What striking botanical contrast establishes the eternal permanence of God's Word against mortal human frailty in Isaiah 40:6-8?
opt1: Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble; he cometh forth like a flower, and is cut down
opt2: All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field: the grass withereth, the flower fadeth: because the spirit of the LORD bloweth upon it: surely the people is grass. The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever
opt3: As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth: for the wind passeth over it, and it is gone
opt4: Heaven and earth shall pass away like smoke, but my words shall not pass away, saith the Holy One of Israel
correct: All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field: the grass withereth, the flower fadeth: because the spirit of the LORD bloweth upon it: surely the people is grass. The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever
explanation: Humanity and worldly empires wither rapidly like parched grass under the desert wind, but God's covenant word endures immutably forever (1 Peter 1:24-25). Isaiah 40:6-8 (KJV) - "All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field: The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: because the spirit of the LORD bloweth upon it: surely the people is grass. The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever."

question: What gentle pastoral tenderness characterizes the sovereign, mighty Lord GOD in Isaiah 40:11?
opt1: He shall guide his people like a king with a golden scepter, and protect their households with an army of angels
opt2: He shall shelter his heritage like an eagle over its nest, and give them to drink of the river of life
opt3: He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young
opt4: He shall lead Joseph like a flock through green pastures, and restore their souls beside the still waters
correct: He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young
explanation: The almighty cosmic Ruler exhibits tender, intimate shepherd care: carrying fragile lambs in His warm bosom and gently leading nursing ewes. Isaiah 40:11 (KJV) - "He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young."

question: What rhetorical cosmic measurement questions illustrate God's unsearchable, infinite greatness in Isaiah 40:12?
opt1: Who hath commanded the morning since his days, and caused the dayspring to know his place in the heavens?
opt2: Who hath shut up the sea with doors when it brake forth, and made the cloud the garment thereof?
opt3: Who hath entered into the springs of the sea, or walked in the search of the depth of the earth?
opt4: Who hath measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and meted out heaven with the span, and comprehended the dust of the earth in a measure, and weighed the mountains in scales, and the hills in a balance?
correct: Who hath measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and meted out heaven with the span, and comprehended the dust of the earth in a measure, and weighed the mountains in scales, and the hills in a balance?
explanation: God holds the oceans in the hollow of His palm, measures the galaxies with the span of His hand, and balances mountain ranges like small weights on scales. Isaiah 40:12 (KJV) - "Who hath measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and meted out heaven with the span, and comprehended the dust of the earth in a measure, and weighed the mountains in scales, and the hills in a balance?"

question: How insignificant are all global nations and superpowers before the majesty of God in Isaiah 40:15, 17?
opt1: Behold, the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance: behold, he taketh up the isles as a very little thing ... All nations before him are as nothing; and they are counted to him less than nothing, and vanity
opt2: The nations are like grasshoppers leaping in the summer heat, and their kings are like dry chaff in the wind
opt3: The kingdoms of the earth are like drops of morning dew upon the thorns, and their armies like mist on the hills
opt4: All the peoples of the world are like clay in the furnace of the potter, and their wealth like broken potsherds
correct: Behold, the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance: behold, he taketh up the isles as a very little thing ... All nations before him are as nothing; and they are counted to him less than nothing, and vanity
explanation: Compared to Yahweh, superpowers are as negligible as a single stray droplet clinging to a bucket or weightless dust on balance scales - literally 'less than nothing and tohu.' Isaiah 40:15, 17 (KJV) - "Behold, the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance: behold, he taketh up the isles as a very little thing ... All nations before him are as nothing; and they are counted to him less than nothing, and vanity."

question: Where does God sit enthroned, and how does He view humanity and the starry heavens in Isaiah 40:22?
opt1: He dwelleth on high above the clouds of Mount Zion, and the princes of the earth are as dust beneath his feet
opt2: It is he that sitteth upon the circle of the earth, and the inhabitants thereof are as grasshoppers; that stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain, and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in
opt3: He rideth upon the wings of the cherubim, and the nations of the world are like sheep scattered in the desert
opt4: He reigneth upon the golden throne of heaven, and the stars are his crown, and the earth his footstool
correct: It is he that sitteth upon the circle of the earth, and the inhabitants thereof are as grasshoppers; that stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain, and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in
explanation: God sits enthroned over the globe ('the circle of the earth'), viewing mortal human beings as tiny grasshoppers, spreading out the vast cosmos like an effortless domestic tent fabric. Isaiah 40:22 (KJV) - "It is he that sitteth upon the circle of the earth, and the inhabitants thereof are as grasshoppers; that stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain, and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in:"

question: How does God manage the countless trillions of stars in the cosmic expanse in Isaiah 40:26?
opt1: He hath set their orbits in the dark void, and commanded them to shine sevenfold until the day of judgment
opt2: He hath measured their light with a golden reed, and weighed their glory in the balances of heaven
opt3: He bringeth out their host by number: he calleth them all by names by the greatness of his might, for that he is strong in power; not one faileth
opt4: He hath appointed twelve constellations to rule the seasons, and no star wandereth from its place
correct: He bringeth out their host by number: he calleth them all by names by the greatness of his might, for that he is strong in power; not one faileth
explanation: Like a celestial general calling the roll, God numbers every star and calls each by its individual name; not a single star is missing or unaccounted for. Isaiah 40:26 (KJV) - "Lift up your eyes on high, and behold who hath created these things, that bringeth out their host by number: he calleth them all by names by the greatness of his might, for that he is strong in power; not one faileth."

question: What unwearied, inexhaustible divine nature answers Israel's complaint that her way is hidden from God in Isaiah 40:28?
opt1: The LORD is righteous in all his ways, and holy in all his works: he slumbereth not neither sleepeth
opt2: The eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to shew himself strong in the behalf of the upright
opt3: The mercy of the LORD is from everlasting to everlasting upon them that fear him, and his truth unto children's children
opt4: Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary? there is no searching of his understanding
correct: Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary? there is no searching of his understanding
explanation: Yahweh never suffers fatigue, exhaustion, or cognitive limitation; His boundless energy and omniscient understanding are beyond human searching. Isaiah 40:28 (KJV) - "Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary? there is no searching of his understanding."

question: What famous climactic promise guarantees supernatural renewal and soaring strength to those who wait upon the LORD in Isaiah 40:29-31?
opt1: He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength ... But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint
opt2: The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree: he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon ... they shall bring forth fruit in old age
opt3: Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding ... it shall be health to thy navel, and marrow to thy bones
opt4: The LORD will give strength unto his people; the LORD will bless his people with peace: they shall conquer all adversaries
correct: He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength ... But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint
explanation: While vigorous human youths exhaust their natural strength and collapse, those who wait expectantly upon Yahweh exchange weakness for divine vigor: soaring like eagles, running tirelessly, and walking without fainting. Isaiah 40:29, 31 (KJV) - "He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength ... But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint."

question: What eastern conqueror is summoned by God to subdue nations, trampling kings like dust before his bow in Isaiah 41:2?
opt1: Who raised up the righteous man from the east, called him to his foot, gave the nations before him, and made him rule over kings? he gave them as the dust to his sword, and as driven stubble to his bow
opt2: Who summoned the prince of Babylon from the river Euphrates to execute vengeance upon the uncircumcised?
opt3: Who called the king of the Medes from the high mountains to break the golden scepter of the Chaldeans?
opt4: Who raised up the champion of Egypt from the cataracts of the Nile to defend the borders of Judah?
correct: Who raised up the righteous man from the east, called him to his foot, gave the nations before him, and made him rule over kings? he gave them as the dust to his sword, and as driven stubble to his bow
explanation: God presents Cyrus the Great (and ultimately Christ), raised from the east to execute divine justice, sweeping away kings like dust and driven chaff. Isaiah 41:2 (KJV) - "Who raised up the righteous man from the east, called him to his foot, gave the nations before him, and made him rule over kings? he gave them as the dust to his sword, and as driven stubble to his bow."

question: What foundational divine self-revelation proclaims God's eternal preexistence and final supremacy over all history in Isaiah 41:4?
opt1: I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end, saith the Lord Almighty
opt2: I the LORD, the first, and with the last; I am he
opt3: I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob forever
opt4: I am that I am: and this is my memorial unto all generations
correct: I the LORD, the first, and with the last; I am he
explanation: Yahweh declares His absolute sovereignty across time: He precedes all historical beginnings ('the first') and outlasts all imperial endings ('with the last; I am he'). Isaiah 41:4 (KJV) - "Who hath wrought and done it, calling the generations from the beginning? I the LORD, the first, and with the last; I am he."

question: What pathetic mutual encouragement among idol manufacturers exposes the anxiety of pagan nations in Isaiah 41:6-7?
opt1: The priests of Baal offered ten thousand rams upon the mountains, and wept before their stone altars
opt2: The kings of the islands assembled their navies and forged bronze armor to face the eastern conqueror
opt3: They helped every one his neighbour; and every one said to his brother, Be of good courage. So the carpenter encouraged the goldsmith, and he that smootheth with the hammer him that smote the anvil, saying, It is ready for the sodering: and he fastened it with nails, that it should not be moved
opt4: The diviners consulted the stars and read the liver omens to predict the day of battle
correct: They helped every one his neighbour; and every one said to his brother, Be of good courage. So the carpenter encouraged the goldsmith, and he that smootheth with the hammer him that smote the anvil, saying, It is ready for the sodering: and he fastened it with nails, that it should not be moved
explanation: Terrified by Cyrus's advance, pagan craftsmen frantically collaborate to manufacture and solder idols, nailing them down so their false gods will not wobble or fall over! Isaiah 41:6-7 (KJV) - "They helped every one his neighbour; and every one said to his brother, Be of good courage. So the carpenter encouraged the goldsmith, and he that smootheth with the hammer him that smote the anvil, saying, It is ready for the sodering: and he fastened it with nails, that it should not be moved."

question: What intimate covenant titles does God bestow upon Israel, identifying her patriarchal heritage in Isaiah 41:8?
opt1: Thou art my holy nation, a royal priesthood, the children of the covenant of David
opt2: Thou art my peculiar treasure, a kingdom of priests, the flock of my pasture
opt3: Thou art my beloved bride, the daughter of Zion, the heritage of my holy mountain
opt4: Thou, Israel, art my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, the seed of Abraham my friend
correct: Thou, Israel, art my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, the seed of Abraham my friend
explanation: God tenderly addresses Israel as His chosen servant, the offspring of Abraham whom He affectionately calls 'my friend' (ohevi). Isaiah 41:8 (KJV) - "But thou, Israel, art my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, the seed of Abraham my friend."

question: What famous promise of divine presence, upholding strength, and personal reassurance is given to Israel in Isaiah 41:10?
opt1: Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness
opt2: The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms: and he shall thrust out the enemy
opt3: The LORD thy God in the midst of thee is mighty; he will save, he will rejoice over thee with joy
opt4: The LORD is on my side; I will not fear: what can man do unto me? the LORD taketh my part
correct: Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness
explanation: God provides fivefold bedrock assurance: His presence ('I am with thee'), His relationship ('I am thy God'), His empowerment ('I will strengthen thee'), His aid ('I will help thee'), and His grip ('I will uphold thee'). Isaiah 41:10 (KJV) - "Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness."

question: To what fragile, despised creature does God compare Israel before promising His divine redemption in Isaiah 41:14?
opt1: Fear not, thou bruised reed of the valley, and ye trembling sheep of the wilderness
opt2: Fear not, thou worm Jacob, and ye men of Israel; I will help thee, saith the LORD, and thy redeemer, the Holy One of Israel
opt3: Fear not, thou little fledgling of the rocks, and ye faint-hearted daughters of Zion
opt4: Fear not, thou dry leaf of the forest, and ye scattered embers of the altar
correct: Fear not, thou worm Jacob, and ye men of Israel; I will help thee, saith the LORD, and thy redeemer, the Holy One of Israel
explanation: Acknowledging Israel's humble, helpless, and downtrodden state ('worm Jacob' / tola'ath), Yahweh reveals Himself as her mighty Redeemer (Go'el), the Holy One of Israel. Isaiah 41:14 (KJV) - "Fear not, thou worm Jacob, and ye men of Israel; I will help thee, saith the LORD, and thy redeemer, the Holy One of Israel."

question: Into what formidable agricultural harvesting implement will God transform helpless Israel in Isaiah 41:15?
opt1: A mighty iron plow that shall turn the rocky hills into fertile fields of grain
opt2: A heavy bronze flail that shall break the gates of the heathen into ten thousand fragments
opt3: Behold, I will make thee a new sharp threshing instrument having teeth: thou shalt thresh the mountains, and beat them small, and shalt make the hills as chaff
opt4: A sharp two-edged sword of victory that shall conquer the kings of the north
correct: Behold, I will make thee a new sharp threshing instrument having teeth: thou shalt thresh the mountains, and beat them small, and shalt make the hills as chaff
explanation: God transforms the worm into an industrial sledge: a new threshing instrument with sharp iron teeth, pulverizing mountainous obstacles into weightless chaff. Isaiah 41:15 (KJV) - "Behold, I will make thee a new sharp threshing instrument having teeth: thou shalt thresh the mountains, and beat them small, and shalt make the hills as chaff."

question: What seven noble trees will God plant together in the barren wilderness to create a magnificent forest in Isaiah 41:19?
opt1: The oak of Bashan, the terebinth of Mamre, the sycamore of the plain, the palm of Jericho, the willow of the brook, the olive of Carmel, and the vine of Sibmah
opt2: The pomegranate of En-gedi, the almond of Bethel, the fig of Bethany, the apple of Sharon, the hyssop of the wall, the cedar of Lebanon, and the cypress of the coast
opt3: The poplar of the valley, the chestnut of the mountains, the hazel of the terraces, the ash of Gilead, the tamarisk of Beersheba, the fir of Hermon, and the olive of Olivet
opt4: I will plant in the wilderness the cedar, the shittah tree, and the myrtle, and the oil tree; I will set in the desert the fir tree, and the pine, and the box tree together
correct: I will plant in the wilderness the cedar, the shittah tree, and the myrtle, and the oil tree; I will set in the desert the fir tree, and the pine, and the box tree together
explanation: Seven diverse trees (cedar, acacia/shittah, myrtle, olive, fir, pine, cypress/box) flourish miraculously side-by-side in arid sands, demonstrating divine creative power. Isaiah 41:19 (KJV) - "I will plant in the wilderness the cedar, the shittah tree, and the myrtle, and the oil tree; I will set in the desert the fir tree, and the pine, and the box tree together:"

question: What courtroom challenge does the King of Jacob issue to pagan manufactured idols in Isaiah 41:21-23?
opt1: Produce your cause, saith the LORD; bring forth your strong reasons, saith the King of Jacob. Let them bring them forth, and shew us what shall happen ... shew the things that are to come hereafter, that we may know that ye are gods: yea, do good, or do evil
opt2: Assemble your priests, saith the Lord of hosts, and call upon your gods to answer by fire upon the altar
opt3: Gather your wise men and astrologers, and declare the dreams of the kings of Babylon
opt4: Weigh your idols in the balances of righteousness, and prove whether their silver can deliver in the day of wrath
correct: Produce your cause, saith the LORD; bring forth your strong reasons, saith the King of Jacob. Let them bring them forth, and shew us what shall happen ... shew the things that are to come hereafter, that we may know that ye are gods: yea, do good, or do evil
explanation: Yahweh challenges pagan gods to an evidentiary trial: prove divinity by accurately predicting future events or performing supernatural acts (good or bad); their total silence exposes them as fraud. Isaiah 41:21-23 (KJV) - "Produce your cause, saith the LORD; bring forth your strong reasons, saith the King of Jacob. Let them bring them forth, and shew us what shall happen: let them shew the former things, what they be, that we may consider them, and know the latter end of them; or declare us things for to come. Shew the things that are to come hereafter, that we may know that ye are gods: yea, do good, or do evil, that we may be dismayed, and behold it together."

question: What final judicial verdict does God render regarding pagan idols and their manufactured images in Isaiah 41:24, 29?
opt1: They are broken cisterns that can hold no water, and their altars are a snare unto the simple
opt2: Behold, ye are of nothing, and your work of nought: an abomination is he that chooseth you ... Behold, they are all vanity; their works are nothing: their molten images are wind and confusion
opt3: They are dead wood covered with gold, and their diviners are blind leaders of the blind
opt4: They are an abomination unto the sanctuary, and their worshippers shall be burned with sulfur
correct: Behold, ye are of nothing, and your work of nought: an abomination is he that chooseth you ... Behold, they are all vanity; their works are nothing: their molten images are wind and confusion
explanation: The divine courtroom reaches its verdict: idols are absolute non-entities ('of nothing'), their works nonexistent, and their metal images mere empty wind and chaos (tohu). Isaiah 41:24, 29 (KJV) - "Behold, ye are of nothing, and your work of nought: an abomination is he that chooseth you ... Behold, they are all vanity; their works are nothing: their molten images are wind and confusion."

question: What opening Servant Song introduces God's chosen Messiah endowed with the Spirit in Isaiah 42:1?
opt1: Behold the Branch of David, whom I have anointed; my righteous King, in whom is my salvation
opt2: Behold my servant, whom I uphold; mine elect, in whom my soul delighteth; I have put my spirit upon him: he shall bring forth judgment to the Gentiles
opt3: Behold the Messenger of the covenant, whom ye delight in; he shall purify the sons of Levi
opt4: Behold the Lamb of God, who taketh away the sin of the world; my holy one from the foundation of the earth
correct: Behold my servant, whom I uphold; mine elect, in whom my soul delighteth; I have put my spirit upon him: he shall bring forth judgment to the Gentiles
explanation: Quoted at Jesus's baptism (Matthew 3:17; 12:18), God introduces the Servant of the LORD (Ebed Yahweh), sustained by the Father, anointed with the Spirit, to establish justice globally. Isaiah 42:1 (KJV) - "Behold my servant, whom I uphold; mine elect, in whom my soul delighteth; I have put my spirit upon him: he shall bring forth judgment to the Gentiles."

question: What gentle, non-violent, and compassionate demeanor characterizes the Servant's ministry in Isaiah 42:2-3?
opt1: He shall march with the sound of a trumpet, and cast down the high towers of the oppressor with fire
opt2: He shall demand absolute obedience in the gates, and break the rebellious with an iron scepter
opt3: He shall not cry, nor lift up, nor cause his voice to be heard in the street. A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench: he shall bring forth judgment unto truth
opt4: He shall not consult with princes, nor regard the rich, but execute vengeance upon the ungodly
correct: He shall not cry, nor lift up, nor cause his voice to be heard in the street. A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench: he shall bring forth judgment unto truth
explanation: The Servant operates without noisy political clamor, tenderly ministering to the damaged and fragile: never snapping a bent reed or extinguishing a flickering, smoking wick (Matthew 12:19-20). Isaiah 42:2-3 (KJV) - "He shall not cry, nor lift up, nor cause his voice to be heard in the street. A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench: he shall bring forth judgment unto truth."

question: What persistent endurance and global Gentile anticipation mark the Servant's mission in Isaiah 42:4?
opt1: He shall not rest until Mount Zion be rebuilt with gold, and the twelve tribes dwell in safety
opt2: He shall not turn back from the cross, until the handwriting of ordinances be blotted out
opt3: He shall not lay down his sword, until all kings of the earth bring tribute unto Jerusalem
opt4: He shall not fail nor be discouraged, till he have set judgment in the earth: and the isles shall wait for his law
correct: He shall not fail nor be discouraged, till he have set judgment in the earth: and the isles shall wait for his law
explanation: The Servant never faints or grows discouraged until international justice is established, with maritime coastlands and Gentile islands eagerly waiting for His instruction (Torah). Isaiah 42:4 (KJV) - "He shall not fail nor be discouraged, till he have set judgment in the earth: and the isles shall wait for his law."

question: What twofold redemptive appointment does God confer upon His Servant in Isaiah 42:6?
opt1: I the LORD have called thee in righteousness, and will hold thine hand, and will keep thee, and give thee for a covenant of the people, for a light of the Gentiles
opt2: For a king over the house of David, and for a high priest after the order of Melchizedek
opt3: For a rock of salvation to the Jews, and for a stumbling stone to the uncircumcised
opt4: For a horn of deliverance to Jacob, and for an ensign of war against the nations
correct: I the LORD have called thee in righteousness, and will hold thine hand, and will keep thee, and give thee for a covenant of the people, for a light of the Gentiles
explanation: The Servant is Himself the covenant incarnate ('a covenant of the people') for Israel and the illuminating revelation of salvation ('a light of the Gentiles') to the entire world. Isaiah 42:6 (KJV) - "I the LORD have called thee in righteousness, and will hold thine hand, and will keep thee, and give thee for a covenant of the people, for a light of the Gentiles;"

question: What liberation mission to the blind and imprisoned defines the Servant's work in Isaiah 42:7?
opt1: To break the bronze gates of Babylon, and lead forth the exiles with silver trumpets
opt2: To open the blind eyes, to bring out the prisoners from the prison, and them that sit in darkness out of the prison house
opt3: To heal the sick of the nations, and wipe away all tears from the mourners of Zion
opt4: To preach the acceptable year of the Lord, and proclaim vengeance upon the heathen
correct: To open the blind eyes, to bring out the prisoners from the prison, and them that sit in darkness out of the prison house
explanation: The Servant delivers humanity from spiritual blindness and the dark, subterranean dungeon of sin and demonic captivity. Isaiah 42:7 (KJV) - "To open the blind eyes, to bring out the prisoners from the prison, and them that sit in darkness out of the prison house."

question: What unshareable divine glory and unique memorial name does God assert against all manufactured idols in Isaiah 42:8?
opt1: I am the Holy One of Israel: my majesty cannot be measured, and my kingdom hath no end
opt2: I am God Almighty: no man can behold my face and live, neither can idols save
opt3: I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images
opt4: I am the King of kings: my throne is established forever, and I will destroy the gods of the earth
correct: I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images
explanation: Yahweh declares His exclusive covenant name ('I am the LORD; that is my name') and His absolute jealousy: He will never share His intrinsic glory or praise with manufactured idols. Isaiah 42:8 (KJV) - "I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images."

question: What warrior imagery depicts God breaking His long silence to conquer His adversaries like a champion in Isaiah 42:13-14?
opt1: The Lord shall descend upon a cloud of fire, and his right hand shall scatter the kings of the earth
opt2: The Almighty shall sound the trumpet of thunder, and the foundations of the mountains shall melt
opt3: The Lord of hosts shall ride upon the whirlwind, and his arrows of lightning shall consume the ungodly
opt4: The LORD shall go forth as a mighty man, he shall stir up jealousy like a man of war: he shall cry, yea, roar; he shall prevail against his enemies. I have long time holden my peace; I have been still, and refrained myself: now will I cry like a travailing woman; I will destroy and devour at once
correct: The LORD shall go forth as a mighty man, he shall stir up jealousy like a man of war: he shall cry, yea, roar; he shall prevail against his enemies. I have long time holden my peace; I have been still, and refrained myself: now will I cry like a travailing woman; I will destroy and devour at once
explanation: After restraining Himself for generations, Yahweh marches forth like an enraged warrior shouting His battle-cry, breathing heavily like a woman in labor to devour His foes. Isaiah 42:13-14 (KJV) - "The LORD shall go forth as a mighty man, he shall stir up jealousy like a man of war: he shall cry, yea, roar; he shall prevail against his enemies. I have long time holden my peace; I have been still, and refrained myself: now will I cry like a travailing woman; I will destroy and devour at once."

question: What gracious guidance and transformation of darkness does God promise to the spiritually blind in Isaiah 42:16?
opt1: I will bring the blind by a way that they knew not; I will lead them in paths that they have not known: I will make darkness light before them, and crooked things straight. These things will I do unto them, and not forsake them
opt2: I will open their understanding through the law of Moses, and will teach them the statutes of the sanctuary
opt3: I will send my angels to carry them across the desert, and will guide them to the springs of Zion
opt4: I will give them a new heart of flesh, and will write my covenant upon the tablets of their soul
correct: I will bring the blind by a way that they knew not; I will lead them in paths that they have not known: I will make darkness light before them, and crooked things straight. These things will I do unto them, and not forsake them
explanation: God tenderly leads the blind along unfamiliar trails, turning their dense darkness into radiant light and smoothing out crooked obstacles with unfailing faithfulness. Isaiah 42:16 (KJV) - "And I will bring the blind by a way that they knew not; I will lead them in paths that they have not known: I will make darkness light before them, and crooked things straight. These things will I do unto them, and not forsake them."

question: What paradoxical spiritual blindness is lamented regarding historical Israel, God's national servant and messenger, in Isaiah 42:19-20?
opt1: Who is rebellious, but the house of Jacob? or stiffnecked, as the seed of Abraham my friend?
opt2: Who is blind, but my servant? or deaf, as my messenger that I sent? who is blind as he that is perfect, and blind as the LORD's servant? Seeing many things, but thou observest not; opening the ears, but he heareth not
opt3: Who hath forgotten the law, but the priests of Levi? or turned to idols, as the kings of Judah?
opt4: Who hath broken the covenant, but the daughter of Zion? or rejected the seers, as the rulers of Jerusalem?
correct: Who is blind, but my servant? or deaf, as my messenger that I sent? who is blind as he that is perfect, and blind as the LORD's servant? Seeing many things, but thou observest not; opening the ears, but he heareth not
explanation: Tragically, while the ideal Messianic Servant (vv. 1-7) brings sight, historical Israel (God's national servant) had eyes but saw nothing, and ears but heard nothing. Isaiah 42:19-20 (KJV) - "Who is blind, but my servant? or deaf, as my messenger that I sent? who is blind as he that is perfect, and blind as the LORD's servant? Seeing many things, but thou observest not; opening the ears, but he heareth not."

question: Who sovereignly gave Jacob for a spoil and Israel to the imperial plunderers, and why, according to Isaiah 42:24-25?
opt1: Was it not the king of Babylon because of his mighty iron chariots and fierce archers?
opt2: Did not the gods of the heathen prevail because the temple altar was broken down in Jerusalem?
opt3: Did not the LORD, he against whom we have sinned? for they would not walk in his ways, neither were obedient unto his law. Therefore he hath poured upon him the fury of his anger, and the strength of battle
opt4: Was it not Pharaoh king of Egypt who betrayed his covenant with the house of David?
correct: Did not the LORD, he against whom we have sinned? for they would not walk in his ways, neither were obedient unto his law. Therefore he hath poured upon him the fury of his anger, and the strength of battle
explanation: Israel's captivity was neither an accident nor the victory of pagan deities; Yahweh Himself handed His people over to plunderers because they persistently disobeyed His law. Isaiah 42:24-25 (KJV) - "Who gave Jacob for a spoil, and Israel to the robbers? did not the LORD, he against whom we have sinned? for they would not walk in his ways, neither were obedient unto his law. Therefore he hath poured upon him the fury of his anger, and the strength of battle: and it hath set him on fire round about, yet he knew not; and it burned him, yet he laid it not to heart."

question: What famous promise of divine companionship and preservation through waters and fire opens Isaiah 43:1-2?
opt1: Fear not, little flock; for it is your Father's good pleasure to deliver you from the snare of the fowler and from the noisome pestilence
opt2: Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest
opt3: Fear not: for I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine. When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee
opt4: The LORD shall preserve thee from all evil: he shall preserve thy soul; the LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in
correct: Fear not: for I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine. When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee
explanation: Yahweh comforts redeemed Israel with personal ownership ('thou art mine') and guarantees that trials of flood and fire will neither overwhelm nor consume her. Isaiah 43:1-2 (KJV) - "Fear not: for I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine. When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee."

question: What three African nations did God give as a geopolitical ransom price for Israel's precious life in Isaiah 43:3-4?
opt1: I gave Babylon for thy ransom, Media and Persia for thy deliverance
opt2: I gave Syria for thy ransom, Philistia and Moab for thy peace
opt3: I gave Tyre for thy ransom, Sidon and Chittim for thy inheritance
opt4: I gave Egypt for thy ransom, Ethiopia and Seba for thee. Since thou wast precious in my sight, thou hast been honourable, and I have loved thee
correct: I gave Egypt for thy ransom, Ethiopia and Seba for thee. Since thou wast precious in my sight, thou hast been honourable, and I have loved thee
explanation: To demonstrate Israel's supreme, precious value in His sight, God compensated the Persian conqueror Cyrus with African territories (Egypt, Cush, Seba). Isaiah 43:3-4 (KJV) - "For I am the LORD thy God, the Holy One of Israel, thy Saviour: I gave Egypt for thy ransom, Ethiopia and Seba for thee. Since thou wast precious in my sight, thou hast been honourable, and I have loved thee: therefore will I give men for thee, and people for thy life."

question: What sole exclusivity of God and Saviourhood is affirmed before the assembled nations in Isaiah 43:10-11?
opt1: Ye are my witnesses, saith the LORD, and my servant whom I have chosen ... before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me. I, even I, am the LORD; and beside me there is no saviour
opt2: I am the Most High God, possessing heaven and earth; and my covenant with Jacob shall never fail
opt3: I am the Holy One of Israel; my throne is from everlasting, and all idols are vanity
opt4: I am the King of kings and Lord of lords; there is no power in heaven or earth that can deliver from my hand
correct: Ye are my witnesses, saith the LORD, and my servant whom I have chosen ... before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me. I, even I, am the LORD; and beside me there is no saviour
explanation: Yahweh declares categorical monotheism: no deity was formed prior to Him, none will ever exist after Him, and outside of Him there is no Saviour whatsoever. Isaiah 43:10-11 (KJV) - "Ye are my witnesses, saith the LORD, and my servant whom I have chosen: that ye may know and believe me, and understand that I am he: before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me. I, even I, am the LORD; and beside me there is no saviour."

question: What new redemptive exodus does God promise to perform, eclipsing the ancient deliverance from Egypt in Isaiah 43:18-19?
opt1: Behold, I will divide the Jordan a second time, and lead my people into the promised land with songs of victory
opt2: Remember ye not the former things, neither consider the things of old. Behold, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth; shall ye not know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert
opt3: Behold, I will bring down manna from heaven, and cause sweet water to flow from the rock in the sight of all nations
opt4: Behold, I will rebuild the walls of Jerusalem with sapphire, and pave the streets of Zion with pure gold
correct: Remember ye not the former things, neither consider the things of old. Behold, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth; shall ye not know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert
explanation: The restoration from Babylon and ultimate Messianic salvation constitute 'a new thing' so magnificent that the original Exodus will be overshadowed by miraculous desert highways and gushing rivers. Isaiah 43:18-19 (KJV) - "Remember ye not the former things, neither consider the things of old. Behold, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth; shall ye not know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert."

question: What primary theological purpose explains why God created and formed the nation of Israel in Isaiah 43:21?
opt1: To conquer the seven nations of Canaan and inherit their cities of stone
opt2: To build an earthly temple of cedar and gold that should endure forever
opt3: This people have I formed for myself; they shall shew forth my praise
opt4: To rule over the kingdoms of the Gentiles with an iron scepter of justice
correct: This people have I formed for myself; they shall shew forth my praise
explanation: Israel's foundational raison d'etre is doxological: uniquely fashioned by God for Himself to declare and reflect His glorious praise to the world. Isaiah 43:21 (KJV) - "This people have I formed for myself; they shall shew forth my praise."

question: How had ungrateful Israel wearied God instead of honoring Him with sacrifices in Isaiah 43:23-24?
opt1: Thou hast offered polluted bread upon mine altar, and brought the blind and the lame for sacrifice
opt2: Thou hast worshipped the golden calf in the wilderness, and burned incense unto the queen of heaven
opt3: Thou hast robbed the sanctuary of its tithes, and perverted judgment in the gates against the fatherless
opt4: Thou hast bought me no sweet cane with money, neither hast thou filled me with the fat of thy sacrifices: but thou hast made me to serve with thy sins, thou hast wearied me with thine iniquities
correct: Thou hast bought me no sweet cane with money, neither hast thou filled me with the fat of thy sacrifices: but thou hast made me to serve with thy sins, thou hast wearied me with thine iniquities
explanation: God never overburdened Israel with excessive ceremonial demands, but Israel burdened and wearied God with her persistent, exhausting transgressions. Isaiah 43:23-24 (KJV) - "Thou hast not brought me the small cattle of thy burnt offerings; neither hast thou honoured me with thy sacrifices ... but thou hast made me to serve with thy sins, thou hast wearied me with thine iniquities."

question: On what gracious basis does God blot out transgressions and forget sins in Isaiah 43:25?
opt1: I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remember thy sins
opt2: For the sake of the covenant which I made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob
opt3: Because of the abundance of the blood of bulls and goats offered upon the altar
opt4: Because of the righteousness of the faithful remnant that prayeth in the temple
correct: I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remember thy sins
explanation: Pardon is entirely unmerited and self-motivated: God blots out iniquities 'for mine own sake' - to vindicate His own holy character, grace, and glory. Isaiah 43:25 (KJV) - "I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remember thy sins."

question: What judicial challenge does God issue to Israel to present her legal defense in Isaiah 43:26?
opt1: Bring forth thy witnesses from among the Gentiles, that they may testify to thy righteousness
opt2: Put me in remembrance: let us plead together: declare thou, that thou mayest be justified
opt3: Weigh thy good deeds against thine iniquities in the balances of the sanctuary
opt4: Recite the statutes of Moses, and prove if thou hast kept the commandments of the Lord
correct: Put me in remembrance: let us plead together: declare thou, that thou mayest be justified
explanation: God summons Israel to a courtroom debate: if she claims innocence or merit, let her state her legal case and present proof to be justified. Isaiah 43:26 (KJV) - "Put me in remembrance: let us plead together: declare thou, that thou mayest be justified."

question: Who was Israel's 'first father' who sinned, establishing her long history of congenital transgression in Isaiah 43:27?
opt1: King Jeroboam the son of Nebat who made Israel to sin with the golden calves
opt2: Aaron the high priest who fashioned the idol while Moses tarried on the mount
opt3: Thy first father hath sinned, and thy teachers have transgressed against me
opt4: King Manasseh who filled Jerusalem with innocent blood and worshipped the host of heaven
correct: Thy first father hath sinned, and thy teachers have transgressed against me
explanation: Israel's ancestral lineage is flawed from the beginning: whether Adam (universal father) or Jacob/Abraham, her earliest patriarchal forebears and prophetic mediators ('teachers') fell into sin. Isaiah 43:27 (KJV) - "Thy first father hath sinned, and thy teachers have transgressed against me."

question: What maritime and military destruction overtakes the Chaldeans in their prized ships in Isaiah 43:14?
opt1: Their galleys shall be shattered upon the rocks of Chittim, and their merchant fleet sunk in the deep
opt2: Their sailors shall weep as they behold the smoke of the golden city burning from afar
opt3: Their canals shall be dried up with sulfur, and their oarsmen shall be led away in chains
opt4: For your sake I have sent to Babylon, and have brought down all their nobles, and the Chaldeans, whose cry is in the ships
correct: For your sake I have sent to Babylon, and have brought down all their nobles, and the Chaldeans, whose cry is in the ships
explanation: For Israel's redemption, God sends conquerors against Babylon, bringing down her fugitive nobles and turning the proud rejoicing of Chaldean mariners into bitter wailing. Isaiah 43:14 (KJV) - "Thus saith the LORD, your redeemer, the Holy One of Israel; For your sake I have sent to Babylon, and have brought down all their nobles, and the Chaldeans, whose cry is in the ships."

question: What affectionate, honorable title is applied to Israel alongside Jacob in Isaiah 44:2?
opt1: Ephraim, my firstborn son
opt2: Zion, the perfection of beauty
opt3: Judah, my royal lawgiver
opt4: Jesurun, whom I have chosen
correct: Jesurun, whom I have chosen
explanation: God addresses Israel as Jesurun ('the Upright One,' poetic title of endearment, Deuteronomy 32:15; 33:5), highlighting the holiness to which she is called. Isaiah 44:2 (KJV) - "Thus saith the LORD that made thee, and formed thee from the womb, which will help thee; Fear not, O Jacob, my servant; and thou, Jesurun, whom I have chosen."

question: What spiritual and agricultural outpouring will cause Israel's offspring to flourish like willows by streams in Isaiah 44:3-4?
